comparison_note: Fourth of six in this group — a sibling to 057's regression-testing question, but using a completely different toolset: 057 built a FULLY CUSTOM pipeline (Step Functions + Lambda + S3 + CloudWatch) because it needed bespoke, structured, clause-level comparison metrics; this one uses the NATIVE Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job service directly, because the requirement (clarity, tone, consistency, brand adherence across a broad validation set) is exactly what Bedrock's built-in evaluation jobs are designed to score — no custom Lambda comparison logic needed. Rule of thumb: general prompt-quality comparison on standard metrics → Bedrock Model Evaluation jobs; custom domain-specific comparison logic (e.g., 'did we miss a specific clause type') → build it yourself in Step Functions. Trap D mirrors 057's trap shape from a different angle: it uses the correct service but skips the actual SIDE-BY-SIDE paired comparison, comparing only the new version against a static baseline instead of running both together under identical conditions.
see_also: 057 (Step Functions custom regression pipeline) is the closest sibling — same goal, different tool choice depending on whether the comparison logic is standard or custom.
explanation: Running Bedrock model evaluation jobs on BOTH the legacy and updated templates across the same comprehensive validation dataset produces measurable, structured quality metrics (clarity, tone, consistency, brand adherence) under identical conditions, and storing both prompt versions plus evaluation outputs in DynamoDB gives a durable, queryable history for automated periodic comparison. B) testing only a small sample and relying on manual comparison misses regressions on broader product lines or edge cases, with no automated or consistent scoring. C) phases in the new template without any structured testing — S3 versioning tracks history but validates nothing. D) uses the right service but evaluates only the NEW template against a static baseline, not a true paired side-by-side run — missing subtle degradations that only show up under identical evaluation conditions.

question: Media platform's generative models produce large volumes of content recommendations and summaries; manual fairness/stereotyping review is impractical. Trust & safety team needs a consistent automated evaluation that identifies biased/unfair patterns across demographic groups, with periodic human spot checks, while reducing judge-model bias and staying aligned with human reviewers.
options: A) Fairness judging pipeline defines scoring prompts, routes outputs through a SINGLE model in Bedrock Prompt Flows; leverages CloudWatch metrics to validate judge consistency INSTEAD OF calibration with human-labeled samples

B) LLM-as-a-judge workflow with structured fairness rubrics evaluated through Bedrock Prompt Flows that orchestrate fairness scoring; use ENSEMBLE judging across MULTIPLE Bedrock models, regularly calibrate judge scores against a HUMAN-LABELED dataset to reduce bias and maintain reviewer alignment

C) LLM-as-a-judge workflow with fairness scoring rubrics evaluated through Bedrock Prompt Flows running a SINGLE high-performing FM; periodically compare judge results with historical fairness thresholds and adjust scoring prompts INSTEAD OF calibration with human-labeled data

D) Bedrock Guardrails blocks outputs containing demographic references or sensitive phrases; CloudWatch alarms let reviewers examine filtered responses, treating filter triggers AS EVIDENCE of fairness compliance
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: Fifth of six in this group, and a different EVALUATION OBJECTIVE than 055-058: those compare two model/prompt VERSIONS against each other (quality regression); this one continuously judges FAIRNESS/BIAS in ongoing GENERATED CONTENT using an LLM-as-a-judge ENSEMBLE, periodically re-anchored against human-labeled ground truth to keep the judge itself from drifting or being biased. Two traps share the same shape (A and C): both use only a SINGLE judge model and skip human calibration entirely, substituting CloudWatch metrics or historical-threshold comparisons instead — automated self-consistency is not the same as staying aligned with real human fairness judgments. Trap D reaches for Bedrock Guardrails, which blocks unsafe content but produces no fairness score and can't detect subtle stereotyping patterns. Compare to 060, which shifts from judging generated TEXT to monitoring the MODEL's decision-pattern bias drift over time, with a different tool (SageMaker Clarify) and a different response (automated remediation, not just scoring).
explanation: Structured fairness rubrics evaluated through Bedrock Prompt Flows give a consistent, repeatable scoring method; using an ENSEMBLE of multiple Bedrock models as judges reduces single-model bias and produces more stable judgments; and regularly calibrating judge scores against a human-labeled dataset keeps the automated pipeline aligned with real reviewer expectations as model behavior evolves. A) and C) both rely on a single judge model and skip human calibration — CloudWatch metrics or historical-threshold comparisons check internal consistency, not alignment with actual human fairness standards, leaving systematic bias undetected. D) Guardrails can block content containing certain terms but generates no fairness score and can't catch subtle stereotyping patterns that don't trip a content filter.

question: Public sector agency uses a generative assistant to draft benefit-eligibility summaries from citizen records. Policy owners are concerned about subtle bias DRIFT over time across demographic groups and require automatic detection, alerting, AND remediation when fairness metrics exceed defined thresholds.
options: A) SageMaker Clarify for PRETRAINING bias analysis, run a WEEKLY batch job checking the INITIAL bias metrics, send results to a DynamoDB table for record keeping; Lambda flags significant changes in the table for any remediation steps

B) SageMaker Clarify with SCHEDULED bias drift monitoring jobs computes fairness and explainability metrics, publishes violations to Amazon EventBridge; EventBridge rules trigger automated remediation workflows in Step Functions that roll back model versions or shift traffic when thresholds are crossed

C) SageMaker Clarify monitoring schedules compute bias metrics and publish results to EventBridge; EventBridge rules send NOTIFICATIONS to administrators, operations team MANUALLY initiates remediation by updating model versions or adjusting traffic weights

D) Daily SageMaker Processing jobs generate bias reports stored in S3; compliance analysts review reports and MANUALLY update the model if metrics show drift; SNS sends email notifications whenever reports are published
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: Sixth of seven in this group, and related to 059 but a different MECHANISM and RESPONSE: 059's LLM-as-a-judge ensemble evaluates individual GENERATED OUTPUTS for stereotyping/fairness with periodic human calibration. This question uses SageMaker Clarify's statistical bias/explainability metrics to monitor the MODEL's decision patterns for demographic disparity DRIFTING over time — a classic ML-fairness monitoring approach — and, critically, requires the detection to trigger AUTOMATED remediation (rollback or traffic-shift via Step Functions), not just an alert. Two traps share the same shape as elsewhere in this exam: C) detects correctly via Clarify+EventBridge but stops at manual notification, and D) skips real drift monitoring entirely for a slower, fully manual daily-report-and-email cycle — both fail the 'automatic detection AND automatic response' requirement, the same manual-remediation trap seen in Group A's circuit-breaker questions (002). 061 closes out the group with a sibling to 059 that uses the SAME Bedrock Model Evaluation service featured in 058's neighbor, but applied to model-CANDIDATE selection instead of prompt-version regression.
explanation: SageMaker Clarify's scheduled bias drift monitoring computes fairness and explainability metrics over time and publishes violations as structured events to EventBridge, which triggers Step Functions remediation workflows that can roll back model versions or shift traffic automatically the moment a threshold is crossed — pairing automated detection with automated corrective action, essential for a sensitive public-sector fairness requirement. A) pretraining-only bias analysis with a weekly check of INITIAL metrics can't detect ongoing drift in a live production system, and DynamoDB-plus-Lambda flagging still leaves remediation to manual intervention. C) correctly wires Clarify to EventBridge for detection but stops at notifying administrators — remediation stays manual, introducing delay and inconsistent enforcement. D) daily batch reports reviewed by compliance analysts, with only SNS email alerts, is a fully manual detection-and-response loop that can let biased behavior persist for extended periods.

question: A legal tech platform wants to measure accuracy, robustness, and reasoning quality across multiple model candidates. The team must approve new foundation models into production only after they pass a consistent and repeatable evaluation cycle, with an automated mechanism that applies controlled metrics, compares multiple candidates side by side, and produces quantifiable scores for decision making.
options: A) Use Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to automatically score multiple model candidates against a curated evaluation dataset

B) Use a Lambda-powered A/B testing framework that routes traffic between multiple model candidates and collects user feedback at RUNTIME; use this feedback to compute the metrics and choose the highest rated model for production approval

C) Use CloudWatch Logs and embed evaluation metadata inside inference logs so engineers can MANUALLY compare hallucination incidents and summarization differences across models; generate NIGHTLY reports from aggregated logs to decide which model to promote

D) Use an internal HUMAN REVIEW process where domain experts score outputs from each model candidate; store reviewer feedback in a structured format and compute aggregate ratings before approving models for production
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: Seventh and last in this group — a close sibling to 058, and both use the SAME underlying Bedrock Model Evaluation service, but applied to a different comparison target. 058 compares OLD vs. NEW PROMPT TEMPLATE versions (paired regression testing before promoting a template). This question compares MULTIPLE FOUNDATION MODEL CANDIDATES against each other on a curated dataset, gating which model earns production approval in the first place — model selection rather than prompt regression. Trap B is a variant of a lesson from earlier in this group: using LIVE user traffic and runtime feedback to decide is an A/B-testing pattern, but it's the wrong tool when the requirement is explicitly PRE-production, repeatable, controlled scoring — exposing real users to unapproved candidates. C and D repeat the 'manual, non-standardized, doesn't scale' pattern seen throughout this group — nightly log reviews and human expert scoring are both inconsistent across reviewers/time and can't produce the quantifiable, repeatable comparison the requirement demands.
explanation: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation provides a managed, automated, repeatable framework that scores multiple foundation model candidates against the same curated evaluation dataset using consistent methodologies, producing quantitative scores for accuracy, robustness, and reasoning quality that make model-to-model comparison objective and auditable — exactly what's needed before approving a new model into a high-stakes legal production environment. B) an A/B test with live traffic and user feedback evaluates models AFTER exposing real users to them, which contradicts the pre-production gating requirement and doesn't guarantee consistent scoring across candidates. C) CloudWatch Logs can store inference data, but computing accuracy/robustness/reasoning quality from it requires manual engineering effort with no built-in standardization — reliability suffers and the process doesn't scale. D) human expert review is valuable but inherently subjective and inconsistent across reviewers and over time, and doesn't scale efficiently across multiple models and large prompt sets the way an automated evaluation pipeline does.

question: A shipping line's route-optimization team already calls Bedrock Runtime via Converse for a future tool-use integration. The assistant must support two production tasks: Q&A over operational procedures and short summarization of port advisories. They must choose an FM available in the deployment REGION, NOT deprecated, COMPATIBLE with the runtime API they use, and justified by BENCHMARK results before implementation.
options: A) Shortlist from the bedrock-mantle /models endpoint using all returned fields; run ONE automatic evaluation job covering BOTH task types
B) Shortlist via ListFoundationModels and GetFoundationModel in the target Region, checking model-specific API compatibility; run SEPARATE automatic evaluation jobs for Q&A and summarization
C) Shortlist from provider model cards; compare THREE candidate models in ONE human evaluation job with FOUR workers per prompt
D) Shortlist text-generation models from ListFoundationModels; treat Converse support as IMPLICIT; run automatic evaluation jobs only for general text generation
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: A new PRE-evaluation step for this group: verifying model availability/deprecation/API-compatibility BEFORE benchmarking, using ListFoundationModels/GetFoundationModel — control-plane discovery, distinct from the bedrock-mantle /models endpoint (trap A, wrong endpoint for a bedrock-runtime Converse integration). Trap C hits documented human-evaluation job limits head-on (max 2 models compared, max 3 workers per prompt); trap D assumes text-generation capability implies Converse compatibility, which is model-specific and not guaranteed.
explanation: ListFoundationModels and GetFoundationModel expose model identifiers, supported modalities/features, and deprecation status in the target Region, letting the team verify runtime-API compatibility before committing; automatic evaluation jobs are organized around ONE task type per job, so running separate jobs for Q&A and summarization mirrors the two actual production workloads rather than a mismatched combined benchmark. A) the bedrock-mantle /models endpoint targets the OpenAI-compatible path, not a bedrock-runtime Converse integration, and a single job can't combine two task types. C) human evaluation jobs are documented to compare up to two models with 1, 2, or 3 workers per prompt — three models and four workers both exceed the limits. D) API support is model-specific; a text-generation capability doesn't guarantee Converse or tool-use compatibility, and evaluating only general text generation doesn't directly benchmark either stated production task.

question: An online university's admissions RAG assistant answers app-deadline/scholarship/residency questions from a 700-prompt S3 JSONL dataset (single-turn retrieval tests + several 4-turn conversations). Separately measure RETRIEVAL quality, GENERATED ANSWER quality, SAFETY risks, and SUBJECTIVE usefulness, avoiding custom pipelines.
options: A) ONE LLM-as-judge evaluation with a generator and separate evaluator model; provide KB responses as bring-your-own inference data; use judge scores for ALL gates
B) ONE retrieve-only RAG evaluation against the FULL dataset (including multi-turn conversations); select response-quality and safety metrics; manually review low scorers
C) ONE retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation against the full dataset; select context relevance, coverage, and response-quality metrics; use scores as the ONLY release gate
D) SPLIT the dataset by purpose: retrieve-only evaluation (single-turn) + retrieve-and-generate evaluation (conversations) + a human-worker evaluation job for subjective review
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: This is the same underlying lesson as 046 in the RAG group (both appeared in the source material describing this exact scenario) — retrieve-only evaluations support only SINGLE-TURN prompts and use ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage, while retrieve-and-generate evaluations use response-quality/safety metrics on up to five turns, and neither substitutes for a genuine human-subjective pass. See 046 for the fuller RAG-architecture framing; this entry anchors the same decision inside the Evaluation group's broader eval-type taxonomy.
explanation: Splitting the dataset lets each managed evaluation mode do the job it's built for: retrieve-only measures retrieved context (ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage) on the single-turn subset, retrieve-and-generate measures generated response quality and safety on the multi-turn conversations, and a human-worker job supplies the subjective usefulness perspective automated metrics can't. B) forcing multi-turn conversations through a retrieve-only job exceeds its documented single-turn support. C) a single retrieve-and-generate job omits the subjective human review entirely. A) LLM-as-judge scores generated responses against an evaluator model but doesn't provide the separate retrieval-quality metrics or genuine human judgment the requirement demands.

question: A maritime logistics team's chatbot uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a custom vector-search KB backed by OpenSearch Serverless. Isolate retrieval from generation, compare RELEVANCE and COVERAGE across a fixed prompt dataset, and preserve enough per-result data to analyze RANKING and LATENCY. Pick two.
options: A) Invoke RetrieveAndGenerate for each benchmark prompt; collect generated citations; compare citation content as the RAW retriever output for per-result ranking analysis
B) Create a RETRIEVE-ONLY RAG evaluation job over the benchmark dataset and review Builtin.ContextRelevance and Builtin.ContextCoverage
C) Increase numberOfResults BEYOND 100 for each query; collect the complete candidate set; treat returned parent/child chunks as fixed-size ranking samples
D) Invoke Retrieve for each benchmark prompt; configure numberOfResults within the supported range; persist retrievalResults content, metadata, location, score, and elapsed request time
E) Create a retrieve-AND-generate RAG evaluation job over the same dataset; use generated response quality as the PRIMARY retriever optimization signal
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: Extends 063's retrieve-only/retrieve-and-generate distinction with the concrete API-level toolkit for isolating the retriever: a raw Retrieve() call harness for per-result score/latency data, PLUS the managed retrieve-only evaluation job for ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage. Trap C hits the documented numberOfResults range (1-100) head-on; traps A and E both confound generation with retrieval — RetrieveAndGenerate's citations don't expose the same score field, and using generated quality as the retriever's PRIMARY signal defeats the isolation goal entirely.
explanation: Calling Retrieve directly (numberOfResults within its documented 1-100 range) and persisting content, metadata, location, score, and elapsed request time isolates the retriever since no FM is invoked to generate an answer; a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job complements this with managed ContextRelevance and ContextCoverage metrics aligned exactly to relevance and coverage. A) RetrieveAndGenerate's output is affected by the generation step and its citations don't expose the same score field Retrieve returns. C) numberOfResults has a documented valid range of 1-100; values beyond that aren't valid, and the actual returned count can be lower than requested (e.g., when hierarchical chunking substitutes parent for child chunks). E) using generated response quality as the PRIMARY retriever signal confounds retriever behavior with prompt and model behavior — exactly what isolation is meant to prevent.

question: A biotech patent team has an offline evaluation dataset with a candidate model's ALREADY-STORED responses in S3. The gate must evaluate SEMANTIC correctness, completeness, and faithfulness of the STORED candidate responses, avoid invoking the candidate model a SECOND TIME, and block deployment if scores fall below baseline.
options: A) LLM-as-judge evaluation using the PRODUCTION BASELINE outputs as the supplied inference response data, with STORED CANDIDATE outputs as referenceResponse (roles reversed)
B) Automatic model evaluation with a custom S3 JSONL dataset that puts STORED CANDIDATE responses in referenceResponse; select question-answering + BERTScore/F1; gate on Completed
C) Enable invocation logging + AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics for staging; run an LLM-as-judge evaluation from the STAGING model configuration (RE-INVOKES); combine with latency/token alarms
D) LLM-as-judge evaluation using the STORED inference response data AS the evaluated responses; select Builtin.Correctness, Builtin.Completeness, Builtin.Faithfulness; gate on Completed
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: A new nuance for this group: LLM-as-judge can evaluate ALREADY-STORED inference response data without re-invoking the target model — a genuine avoid-double-invocation optimization, distinct from every other member's live-invocation evaluation flows. Trap A is the sharpest: it reverses WHICH response is being evaluated (scoring the baseline against the candidate as reference, backwards from what's needed). Trap B treats candidate responses as ground-truth reference data rather than the thing being scored. Trap C defeats the whole point by re-invoking via the staging model configuration.
explanation: When inference response data is supplied in the prompt dataset, Bedrock's LLM-as-judge evaluation scores THAT supplied data instead of invoking the target model again, and the built-in judge metrics Builtin.Correctness, Builtin.Completeness, and Builtin.Faithfulness map directly to semantic correctness, completeness, and grounding — with results written asynchronously to S3, letting a deployment gate wait for Completed status before checking scores. A) reverses the roles — scoring production baseline outputs against candidate outputs as reference answers the wrong question. B) automatic evaluation with candidate responses placed in referenceResponse treats them as ground truth rather than the responses being evaluated. C) running the evaluation from a staging model configuration re-invokes the candidate model, which the requirement explicitly avoids.

question: A boutique travel marketplace's itinerary-planning assistant shows acceptable OFFLINE factual accuracy, but production users report responses are UNHELPFUL, too VERBOSE, or poorly matched to travel PREFERENCES. Continuously improve model-selection decisions with a user-centered mechanism, without building a custom ML scoring pipeline.
options: A) In-product ratings/comments stored with prompt/response metadata; Bedrock model evaluations with HUMAN WORKERS to compare candidate model configurations
B) Guardrail intervention tracking; store blocked prompt/response events; use POLICY VIOLATION RATES to select model configurations
C) Response latency and token-count dashboards; store operational metrics with model IDs; use CloudWatch alarms to select model configurations
D) In-product ratings/comments stored with metadata; use ONLY AUTOMATED Bedrock metrics (no human judgment) to select model configurations
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: A new SUBJECTIVE-quality angle for this group: captures live user feedback as an evaluation dataset, then uses Bedrock's HUMAN-WORKER evaluation mode — appropriate specifically because helpfulness/verbosity/preference-fit are subjective criteria that automated scoring alone (trap D) can't reliably capture. Traps B and C both mistake OPERATIONAL signals (safety interventions, latency/tokens) for user-perceived QUALITY — a model can pass every safety and performance check while still producing unhelpful responses.
explanation: Capturing in-product ratings and comments alongside prompt/response metadata preserves the context needed to analyze WHY users preferred or rejected outputs, and Bedrock model evaluations with human workers directly measure subjective criteria like helpfulness, tone, and preference fit when comparing candidate model configurations. B) guardrail intervention rates measure safety/compliance, not general user satisfaction — a model can have low violation rates while still being unhelpful or verbose. C) latency and token metrics measure system behavior, not whether users found an answer useful. D) automated metrics alone aren't enough when the core concern is subjective, user-perceived quality that needs human judgment in the evaluation step itself.

question: A scholarship foundation's assistant drafts eligibility explanations. The team has an offline dataset varying DEMOGRAPHIC PROXIES (names, ages, locations) while keeping scholarship facts constant. Compare PROMPT VERSIONS before deployment, generate AUDITABLE COHORT-LEVEL fairness measurements, and minimize custom evaluation logic.
options: A) Separate Bedrock model evaluation jobs per candidate prompt (NOT versioned in Prompt Management), same dataset/rubric, export summaries as CloudWatch custom metrics
B) Version candidate prompts in Prompt Management; run the dataset through Bedrock Flows with a Bedrock-hosted LLM-as-judge step; publish COHORT DISPARITY scores as CloudWatch custom metrics
C) Version candidate prompts in Prompt Management; run through Flows; route outputs to Amazon A2I HUMAN reviewers; publish adjudicated cohort scores
D) Version candidate prompts in Prompt Management; run through Flows with LLM-judge; publish OVERALL/AGGREGATE fairness pass rates (not cohort-level)
group: Evaluation, A/B Testing, Rollout & Regression Frameworks
comparison_note: Extends this group's existing bias/fairness member with a cleaner three-part toolkit — Prompt Management for VERSIONED prompt artifacts (audit trail), Flows for repeatable orchestration, LLM-as-judge for the qualitative fairness rubric — and a sharp new trap: aggregating the fairness signal across the WHOLE dataset (trap D) can hide exactly the cohort-level disparities the requirement asks to measure. Trap C's human-adjudication path can improve judgment quality but adds more reviewer-management overhead than the 'minimize custom evaluation logic' constraint wants.
explanation: Prompt Management turns candidate prompts into versioned, managed resources rather than ad hoc strings, strengthening the audit trail for which exact version produced which cohort result; Bedrock Flows orchestrates the repeatable evaluation path, and an LLM-as-judge step scores outputs against a fairness rubric — with results published as cohort-level CloudWatch custom metrics so disparities across demographic proxy groups stay visible rather than averaged away. A) doesn't tie prompts to managed Prompt Management versions, weakening the audit trail for which artifact produced which result. C) human adjudication can improve judgment quality but adds workflow and reviewer-management overhead beyond what's needed here. D) aggregating into overall pass rates instead of preserving cohort structure can hide exactly the disparities the requirement asks to surface.

question: Media company's Bedrock content generation hits 'Too many requests' throttling during regional traffic spikes. Need more resilience WITHOUT changing app logic or switching model families.
options: A) CloudFront edge distribution layer in front of Bedrock calls from all Regions
B) Increase provisioned inference units in a single Region + rely on autoscaling for peak load from other Regions
C) Enable Bedrock cross-Region inference so requests auto-failover to another Region when the primary Region throttles
D) Step Functions workflow retries failed invocations with exponential backoff, replays until throttling clears
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: First of seven 'too many requests / capacity mismatch' questions. Here the workload is still REAL-TIME/interactive across multiple regions — the fix keeps the same latency profile but adds Regional failover using Bedrock's OWN BUILT-IN cross-Region inference feature, with zero application-level routing changes. Contrast with 069, where the workload is actually a BATCH job with relaxed latency — the fix there isn't failover, it's switching the endpoint TYPE from real-time/synchronous to asynchronous. 070 pushes the same batch-tolerant scenario further with request batching for GPU utilization. 071 is the sharpest contrast: it needs a fully CUSTOM, application-level multi-Region architecture (Route 53 health checks/failover) for a PROLONGED FULL OUTAGE plus compliance routing — a bigger problem than Bedrock's native cross-Region inference alone solves. 072 protects Bedrock at a different LAYER entirely — the API Gateway edge, before requests even reach a backend. 073 adds a further capacity lever (reserved provisioned throughput for predictable real-time performance), and 074 revisits the API Gateway edge from 072's angle but for request-diagnostics rather than throttling.
explanation: Bedrock cross-Region inference automatically routes requests to a secondary Region when the primary hits throttling/capacity limits — no app-logic changes, same model family preserved, failover managed transparently at the Bedrock level. A) CloudFront can't reduce dynamic, per-request model inference throttling — adds complexity with no real benefit. B) single-Region provisioned capacity doesn't help when that Region itself is throttling, and raises cost. D) retry/backoff via Step Functions adds latency and doesn't guarantee availability during a genuine regional capacity shortage — it just waits longer for the same constrained Region.

question: Nightly content-moderation batch job (millions of posts, not user-facing, hours-long window acceptable) currently uses a real-time SageMaker endpoint that scales sharply and throttles during the batch window, driving up cost. Redesign for the relaxed latency requirement.
options: A) Bigger instances + higher max instance count on the current real-time endpoint, aggressive scale-out during the nightly window, reserved instances/savings plans to offset cost
B) Keep the real-time endpoint, front it with an SQS queue drained by Lambda functions sending SYNCHRONOUS requests, rely on Auto Scaling to rapidly expand instance count during the window

C) Replace with Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput for dedicated capacity, process all posts in real time during the batch window, increase provisioned units at peak, CloudWatch alarms for throttling

D) SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoint reads payloads from S3, processes in the background, writes results to S3 output; use a queue/scheduled process to upload nightly batches so the endpoint scales gradually
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Second of five — pairs with 068. This is the RELAXED-LATENCY case: 'completing within several hours is acceptable' is the tell. The fix isn't more capacity or failover, it's changing the invocation MODEL entirely (sync real-time → async, S3-backed), though it still processes one item per call. Trap options A and B both keep the synchronous real-time endpoint (just make it bigger, or add a queue in front of it) — neither changes the fundamental cost/throttling profile. 070 pushes this same batch-tolerant scenario one step further: once you're on the right endpoint type, GROUPING records into each call (batching) is the next lever for GPU utilization.
explanation: SageMaker asynchronous inference reads inputs from S3 and processes in the background, smoothing load and avoiding per-request throttling spikes that synchronous endpoints hit — ideal for large, time-flexible batch workloads, letting the team tune concurrency/scaling to match cost targets. A) and B) both keep the endpoint synchronous and real-time — they still have to absorb a concentrated burst of millions of requests, recreating the same scaling/cost/throttling problem. C) Bedrock provisioned throughput is built for predictable, steady, low-latency traffic — spinning it up for a short nightly window to force real-time processing of a genuinely batch-tolerant workload is expensive and doesn't exploit the relaxed latency requirement at all.

question: Media moderation system runs hourly batch jobs sending tens of thousands of content snippets through a foundation model, one inference request per item, leading to underutilized GPU instances, high costs, and jobs that occasionally miss their completion windows during traffic spikes. Redesign using batching strategies and high-throughput inference to maximize utilization and throughput.
options: A) SageMaker Processing jobs distribute the moderation workload across multiple nodes, each node calls the FM endpoint in PARALLEL; rely on the distributed processing cluster to finish faster WITHOUT changing the per-item invocation pattern

B) Increase the number of GPU instances on the EXISTING real-time endpoint, scale to MAXIMUM size available; rely on additional capacity to absorb spikes WITHOUT modifying request pattern or batching behavior

C) Configure a SageMaker real-time endpoint with LARGER instance types, enable request-level parallelism by submitting multiple CONCURRENT mini-batches across several threads; rely on endpoint invocation concurrency to SIMULATE high throughput WITHOUT adopting full batch transform or asynchronous inference

D) Configure a high-throughput inference setup using SageMaker BATCH TRANSFORM or SageMaker ASYNCHRONOUS INFERENCE, submit LARGE BATCHES that group multiple records per request; use AUTO SCALING rules on the model endpoint to match peak batch volumes and keep GPU instances fully utilized
domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Apps
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Third in this group, and a distinct nuance from 069: that question fixed THROTTLING by switching a real-time endpoint to async for a batch-tolerant workload, but still processed one item per call. This question's core problem is different — GPU UNDERUTILIZATION from one-item-per-request overhead, even without necessarily throttling — so the fix is REQUEST BATCHING (grouping many records into each inference call) via batch transform or async inference, plus auto scaling to match volume. Every wrong option here keeps the one-item-per-call pattern intact (more nodes, more instances, or more concurrent threads) without ever grouping records into larger batches — that's the tell distinguishing 'needs more capacity' from 'needs batching.'
explanation: SageMaker batch transform or asynchronous inference, configured to group multiple content snippets into each inference request, lets every GPU process a larger effective workload per call instead of paying per-request overhead thousands of times over; auto scaling then matches instance count to queued/batch volume, keeping utilization high and the job within its completion window. A) distributing across more Processing job nodes only adds parallelism at the orchestration layer — the model endpoint still receives one item per call, so it remains the bottleneck. B) more GPU instances on the same real-time endpoint raises cost without touching the root inefficiency: small, unbatched requests. C) concurrent mini-batches across threads on a real-time endpoint still send many small calls and hit the endpoint's built-in concurrency/latency constraints — it mimics throughput without the efficiency of true batch processing.

question: Global healthcare analytics company's clinical summarization system currently runs in a single Region. New regulatory and availability requirements mandate it remain fully functional even if one Region experiences a PROLONGED outage, while routing requests according to regional compliance rules. Design a multi-Region architecture supporting active-active or active-passive deployment, automated health checks, and safe traffic redirection during failures.
options: A) Run the Bedrock workload in ONE Region, enable cross-Region data replication only, direct all inference requests through a SINGLE Route 53 simple record; rely on DNS caching for failover, no health checks or routing policies

B) Deploy the Bedrock-based inference workflow in TWO Regions, expose each through separate regional endpoints registered in Route 53 using FAILOVER or LATENCY-BASED routing; configure Route 53 HEALTH CHECKS to monitor each endpoint and automatically redirect traffic to the healthy Region during outages

C) Create separate Bedrock endpoints in multiple Regions, configure Route 53 with WEIGHTED routing that ALWAYS favors the primary Region regardless of health status; traffic shifts back only after administrators MANUALLY update routing weights following an outage

D) Deploy the Bedrock workflow in two Regions but front both with a SINGLE Route 53 record using simple routing and NO health checks; application clients detect endpoint failures and MANUALLY shift requests to the secondary Region
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Fourth of five in this group, and a sharp contrast with 068: that question used Bedrock's BUILT-IN cross-Region inference (a Bedrock-managed capability) to auto-failover during THROTTLING, with zero application-layer routing changes. This question needs a fully custom, application-level multi-Region architecture — two independently deployed Bedrock workflows, each behind its own Route 53 endpoint, with EXPLICIT failover/latency-based routing and health checks — because the requirement here is broader: surviving a PROLONGED FULL REGIONAL OUTAGE plus enforcing region-specific COMPLIANCE routing, not just smoothing over transient capacity throttling. Rule of thumb: transient throttling within Bedrock's control → let Bedrock's native cross-Region inference handle it (068); a true multi-Region disaster-recovery/compliance-routing architecture spanning independently deployed workflows → build it yourself with Route 53 (071).
explanation: Deploying the inference workflow in two Regions, each behind its own Route 53 endpoint, with failover or latency-based routing policies and active health checks, gives automated, hands-off traffic redirection the moment a Region becomes unhealthy — meeting both the business-continuity requirement (survive a prolonged outage) and the regulatory requirement (region-aware routing). A) replicating only data while running inference in a single Region, behind a simple DNS record with no health checks, means there is no mechanism to redirect traffic away from a failed Region at all. C) weighted routing that always favors the primary Region regardless of health status can't detect or react to an outage — traffic keeps flowing to the dead Region until a human intervenes. D) a single simple DNS record with no health checks and reliance on client-side manual failover pushes failure detection onto every client and introduces unpredictable, inconsistent behavior during a regional outage.

question: SaaS provider exposes a text analysis API to hundreds of external customers, internally calling Amazon Bedrock for classification and sentiment analysis. Some customers send prompts exceeding token limits or omit required fields; others generate sudden traffic spikes overloading the downstream model endpoint. Need strict schema validation for request bodies/parameters AND tiered throttling per customer plan, BEFORE any request reaches Bedrock. Pick two.
options: A) API Gateway with a Lambda integration that performs ALL request validation INSIDE the function code, relies on CloudWatch alarms to detect customers exceeding token limits or sending malformed payloads
B) Configure API Gateway with request validators and models using JSON Schema to enforce required fields and token-limit constraints on the API BEFORE invoking the Lambda function that calls Bedrock

C) Application Load Balancer + AWS WAF with rate-based rules to block high request rates from abusive clients; rely on the downstream Lambda function calling Bedrock to handle JSON parsing, required-field checks, and token-limit enforcement for ALL customers
D) Use API keys and usage plans in API Gateway to define per-customer throttling limits for each subscription tier so traffic is controlled before it reaches the downstream model endpoint
E) Implement throttling with Lambda reserved concurrency so burst traffic is absorbed by the function
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Fifth of seven in this group, and a different LAYER than 068-071: those all manage capacity/failover AT or AFTER the Bedrock/SageMaker endpoint (Regional failover, endpoint type, batching, multi-Region DR). This question protects Bedrock from ever seeing the problem in the first place — rejecting malformed/oversized requests and shaping per-customer traffic entirely at the API GATEWAY edge, before any backend compute (Lambda or Bedrock) runs. Two traps share a pattern: A) and C) both push validation and/or throttling logic downstream into Lambda or rely on reactive detection (CloudWatch alarms, WAF rate limiting) instead of rejecting bad requests up front and enforcing per-tenant quotas at the edge. 074 uses this exact same API Gateway + Lambda toolkit for a different goal — catching structurally malformed requests for clean debugging rather than throttling traffic — and 073 closes the group with a proactive capacity-reservation strategy (Bedrock provisioned throughput) for real-time workloads.
explanation: API Gateway request validators with JSON Schema models reject malformed payloads and enforce field/token-limit constraints before any Lambda or Bedrock invocation happens, protecting the backend and simplifying error handling; API keys and usage plans then let the provider define distinct throttling/quota tiers per customer subscription, enforced directly at the API edge before traffic ever reaches the model endpoint. A) pushes all validation into Lambda code — invalid requests still consume compute and reach the integration layer, and CloudWatch alarms only detect problems after they've already happened. C) WAF rate-based rules can block abusive traffic patterns but provide no JSON Schema validation or per-tenant usage plans, leaving field/token checks to the downstream Lambda. E) Lambda reserved concurrency absorbs bursts but offers no per-customer differentiation or tiered limits — it's a blunt instrument, not tenant-aware throttling.

question: A global enterprise operates a customer support assistant used across mobile and web platforms. Traffic fluctuates sharply throughout the day and surges heavily during promotions and seasonal events, causing throttling and slow response times. Finance needs predictable monthly spending, while product owners require consistently fast responses even during peak demand.
options: A) Use Amazon Bedrock on-demand APIs and set HIGH retry and timeout values to smooth out throttling during peak traffic periods; enable CloudWatch alarms on latency and continue increasing memory in application clients to improve response predictability

B) Configure Lambda functions to invoke Bedrock on-demand APIs for all requests and reserve HIGH Lambda memory sizes to optimize throughput; depend on AWS Lambda scaling to absorb burst traffic instead of adjusting model capacity

C) Deploy the model on SageMaker AI real-time endpoints with a MINIMAL instance size and rely on auto scaling to handle all peak loads; increase concurrent invocation limits on the application side to let the endpoint scale REACTIVELY during seasonal promotions

D) Use Amazon Bedrock PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT to provide dedicated model capacity for peak demand and configure tokens-per-second allocation based on expected surge patterns; monitor utilization with CloudWatch and adjust provisioned units to maintain fast responses during traffic spikes
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Sixth of seven in this group, and a different LEVER than everything before it: 068 reroutes to another Region when throttled (real-time, reactive failover); 069/070 shift to async/batch endpoints and request-batching (accept relaxed latency for batch-tolerant work); 071 handles a full regional OUTAGE via multi-Region DR; 072/074 gatekeep at the API edge before Bedrock is even called. This question is about RESERVING dedicated capacity up front via Bedrock provisioned throughput, so a REAL-TIME, latency-sensitive workload gets consistently fast responses even through sharp, somewhat-predictable surges — a proactive capacity-reservation strategy rather than a reactive or relaxed-latency one. All three wrong options keep the workload on SHARED, on-demand capacity and try to compensate around the edges — bigger retries/timeouts, more Lambda concurrency, or reactive auto scaling on undersized instances — none of which changes the fact that the underlying model capacity is still shared and can still throttle or start slow exactly when it's needed most.
explanation: Bedrock provisioned throughput reserves dedicated model capacity — sized in tokens per second based on expected surge patterns — so the workload is never subject to shared on-demand throttling, giving both predictable performance during traffic spikes and predictable cost for finance, since the reserved capacity has a known price regardless of exact traffic; CloudWatch utilization monitoring lets the team right-size provisioned units over time. A) and B) both stay on shared on-demand capacity — retries, timeouts, client memory tuning, and Lambda scaling can't eliminate throttling caused by shared model-layer capacity limits, and can increase cost without improving predictability. C) a minimal SageMaker instance size creates its own latency and slow cold-start problems, and reactive auto scaling only kicks in AFTER load has already increased, causing exactly the delay and throttling during sudden demand spikes the requirement wants eliminated.

question: A customer support application intermittently returns generic 'model invocation failed' errors when sending structured JSON prompts to a foundation model API. Initial checks reveal that some requests include optional fields in unexpected formats and unescaped characters that were not present during earlier testing.
options: A) Implement an Amazon SQS buffering layer that queues all incoming requests and use a Lambda consumer to NORMALIZE field names before invoking the model API; depend on SQS dead letter queues to capture malformed payloads that cannot be processed successfully

B) Implement SCHEMA VALIDATION in Amazon API Gateway using request models to enforce strict JSON structure and run a Lambda PREPROCESSOR that sanitizes and escapes user-supplied fields before calling the foundation model; capture detailed validation failures and preprocessing errors in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to provide clear diagnostics for debugging issues

C) Configure Amazon API Gateway to perform basic request PASSTHROUGH and add a Lambda function that escapes special characters before invoking the foundation model API; log the preprocessing results in CloudWatch Logs to help identify faulty payloads during troubleshooting

D) Send all requests directly to the model endpoint and customize the foundation model itself to reject malformed fields; enable CloudWatch metric filters to alert developers whenever the model responds with an invocation error
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: Seventh and last in this group, and closely related to 072 in TOOL (API Gateway request validators with JSON Schema models) but different in GOAL: 072 enforces required fields/token limits paired with tiered, PER-CUSTOMER USAGE PLANS to throttle and protect a multi-tenant external API from cost/abuse. This question uses the same schema-validation mechanism paired with a Lambda SANITIZATION/ESCAPING preprocessor purely to catch STRUCTURALLY MALFORMED requests (unexpected optional-field formats, unescaped characters) before they cause an opaque 'model invocation failed' error — the goal here is DEBUGGABILITY and clean error diagnostics, not throttling or quota enforcement. Trap C looks similar (also API Gateway + Lambda) but runs API Gateway in PASSTHROUGH mode (no real schema validation) and only escapes characters — structural problems like invalid nesting or wrong types still reach the model undetected. Trap D repeats a recurring lesson: don't rely on the FM itself to enforce structure — models don't guarantee strict schema rejection, and CloudWatch metric filters on invocation errors are purely reactive, offering little diagnostic clarity.
explanation: API Gateway request models enforce strict JSON schema validation — rejecting malformed structure, wrong types, and missing or misshapen optional fields before the request ever reaches compute — and a Lambda preprocessing layer sanitizes and escapes user-supplied content as an additional safeguard before the foundation model is ever called; capturing both validation failures and preprocessing errors in CloudWatch Logs turns a generic 'model invocation failed' into an actionable, specific diagnostic. A) SQS buffering with a Lambda consumer that only normalizes field NAMES doesn't validate nested JSON structure or escape characters, so malformed payloads still reach the model — a dead-letter queue only tells you something failed after the fact, not why. C) running API Gateway in passthrough mode skips real schema validation entirely, leaving structural correctness solely to a Lambda function that only escapes characters — invalid nesting or incorrect field types still slip through undetected. D) expecting the foundation model itself to reject malformed fields is unreliable since models don't guarantee strict validation behavior, and CloudWatch metric filters on invocation errors are reactive alerts, not upfront prevention or clear root-cause diagnostics.

question: A biotech diagnostics lab's clinical AI platform shows repeated InvocationThrottles during predictable shift-change bursts, though Lambda stays below timeout/concurrency limits. Compliance requires all inference to STAY IN the current Region; the team wants to keep using the Bedrock runtime API without managing model servers. The model has a supported dedicated-capacity offering; AWS Support approved capacity units; procurement approved a ONE-MONTH commitment.
options: A) Call CreateProvisionedModelThroughput with the contextual variant model ID, approved modelUnits, OneMonth commitmentDuration; then invoke PROVISIONEDMODELARN as modelId
B) Call CreateProvisionedModelThroughput as above; then invoke the BASE MODEL ID (not the returned ARN)
C) Raise Lambda concurrency/timeout settings; keep invoking the base model ID; retry throttled requests with exponential backoff
D) Create an APPLICATION INFERENCE PROFILE for the same in-Region model; invoke the profile ID as modelId
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: The API-MECHANICS companion to this group's existing Provisioned Throughput member: same underlying capacity lever, but the exact API sequence matters — CreateProvisionedModelThroughput returns a provisionedModelArn that MUST be used as modelId at invocation time (trap B invokes the base model ID instead, silently bypassing the reserved capacity entirely). Trap D repeats a documented limitation: inference profiles currently do NOT support Provisioned Throughput.
explanation: CreateProvisionedModelThroughput (with provisionedModelName, the supported model ID, approved modelUnits, and OneMonth commitmentDuration) provisions dedicated in-Region Bedrock throughput while keeping the managed runtime API — the application just needs to invoke the RETURNED provisionedModelArn as modelId once the resource reaches InService. B) invoking the base model ID after provisioning capacity means the runtime request never uses the reserved capacity — the ARN is required. C) Lambda concurrency/timeout settings affect the wrapper, not downstream Bedrock capacity, and retries mitigate transient throttling without solving predictable sustained bursts. D) application inference profiles help with cost/usage tracking, but AWS documents that inference profiles currently do not support Provisioned Throughput.

question: A credit union's live chat assistant uses Amazon Nova Pro via a supported CROSS-REGION inference profile in a US Region and wants LOWER LATENCY for interactive requests, keeping the same FM/integration, WITHOUT changing Bedrock service tiers or buying reserved capacity. If the latency-optimized quota is reached, the team prefers normal processing rather than outright failure.
options: A) Set maxTokens LOWER on each request; inspect token count metrics for shorter responses
B) Set performanceConfig.latency to OPTIMIZED on each supported inference request; inspect the response and CloudTrail to confirm served configuration
C) Leave performanceConfig.latency at STANDARD; enable response STREAMING to return tokens progressively
D) Set performanceConfig.latency=optimized ONLY on the FIRST request in each chat session, assuming later turns inherit it
domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Apps
group: Throttling, Capacity & Batch Inference Design
comparison_note: A distinct LATENCY lever from this group's other capacity/throughput members — performanceConfig.latency is a PER-REQUEST setting (not a capacity purchase or a service-tier change), with documented graceful fallback to Standard when its own quota is exhausted. Trap D is the sharpest new nuance: latency optimization must be set on EVERY supported request, since each conversational turn is a separate inference call — setting it only once does not carry forward to later turns.
explanation: performanceConfig.latency=optimized requests the Bedrock preview latency-optimized inference path per call for supported models/profiles, with no model retraining, service-tier change, or dedicated capacity purchase; if the latency-optimized quota is reached, Bedrock automatically falls back to Standard latency (billed at Standard rates) rather than failing, and the served configuration is visible in the response and CloudTrail. A) lower maxTokens can shorten output but doesn't request the documented optimization path. C) streaming improves PERCEIVED responsiveness but doesn't itself request optimized latency, and leaving the setting at standard means Bedrock defaults to Standard latency. D) each chat turn is a separate inference request, so setting the flag only once does not apply to subsequent turns.

question: Financial services GenAI assistant on Bedrock processes highly sensitive transaction/dispute data. Security requires ALL Bedrock traffic to stay inside the AWS network, with only specific application subnets able to call the Bedrock APIs — no public internet exposure — while scaling across multiple AZs.
options: A) Create a VPC endpoint service for the application, security groups restrict connecting subnets, access via internal DNS rules
B) Interface VPC endpoints for Bedrock via AWS PrivateLink + tightly scoped security groups allowing only approved application subnets, deployed across multiple AZs
C) Interface VPC endpoints for Bedrock, security groups allow access from ALL subnets in the VPC for simplicity, multi-AZ, default VPC routing
D) NAT gateway for all outbound Bedrock calls, NAT access restricted to application subnets, cross-AZ failover via extra route table entries
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: First of six in this group — pairs with 078 (identity/authZ path), 079 (tenant/data isolation via Bedrock Knowledge Bases), 080 (fine-grained Lake Formation governance for a single org's regulated data), 081 (OpenSearch Serverless multi-tenant vector isolation), and 082 (cross-account vector retrieval without data duplication). This question locks down the NETWORK path to Bedrock (PrivateLink interface endpoints, scoped security groups) — WHERE the traffic can flow.
explanation: Interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) keep all Bedrock traffic inside the AWS network end-to-end, and security groups scoped to only the approved application subnets satisfy the least-privilege isolation requirement while scaling cleanly across AZs. A) 'VPC endpoint service' is the wrong direction entirely — that construct is for exposing YOUR OWN app as a service to other VPCs (provider side of PrivateLink), it can't front a managed AWS service like Bedrock. C) uses the right mechanism (interface VPC endpoint) but opens security groups to all subnets — violates the 'only approved application subnets' requirement even though traffic stays private. D) NAT gateway routes through a public-network-adjacent path and can't enforce endpoint-level access restrictions the way a PrivateLink interface endpoint can.

question: Healthcare provider exposes internal FM endpoints to clinicians through existing web apps that already authenticate against an enterprise identity provider. Security wants to federate identities into AWS, enrich tokens with department/role info, enforce least privilege on FM APIs based on user attributes AND request context (time of day, source network), and centralize authorization — all WITHOUT modifying existing login flows.
options: A) Amazon Cognito with SAML federation to the enterprise identity provider + pre-token-generation Lambda triggers to enrich tokens with department/role attributes; IAM policies with condition keys for source IP and time-based controls enforce least privilege on FM APIs

B) IAM Identity Center with automatic user provisioning, map enterprise roles directly to IAM roles for FM access; enforce time-based and network-based restrictions using service control policies on clinician organizational units

C) Amazon Cognito user pools as the PRIMARY identity provider for all applications, MIGRATE clinician identities from the enterprise provider; resource-based policies on FM endpoints + security group rules for access control

D) API Gateway custom authorizers validate tokens issued by the enterprise identity provider, attach model access permissions directly to each API method; manage clinician attributes in DynamoDB tables, perform attribute checks inside Lambda authorizers
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Second of four — pairs with 077 (network path). That question locks down WHERE traffic can flow; this one locks down WHO can call it — federating existing enterprise logins via SAML into Cognito, enriching tokens with department/role via a pre-token-generation Lambda, then using IAM policy condition keys (source IP, time-of-day) for fine-grained, context-aware least privilege. Compare to 079 and 080, which handle DATA-level isolation (tenant separation, fine-grained field permissions) rather than network or identity.
explanation: Cognito with SAML federation integrates with the existing enterprise identity provider without requiring any changes to how clinicians log in, and a pre-token-generation Lambda trigger enriches tokens with trusted department/role metadata before they're used for authorization. IAM policies with context-based condition keys (source IP, time of day, department attributes) then enforce fine-grained least privilege on FM API access, centralizing authorization decisions without touching the legacy login flow. B) IAM Identity Center doesn't fit when authentication already happens through an external IdP that can't be rewritten, and SCPs can't enforce per-request, context-aware authorization at the individual API-call level. C) migrating clinicians into a new Cognito pool breaks the 'preserve existing login flows' requirement entirely, and resource-based policies/security groups don't offer department- or context-based fine-grained control. D) API Gateway custom authorizers plus manual DynamoDB attribute storage add operational overhead and don't natively integrate with enterprise federation or token enrichment.

question: SaaS provider builds a conversational assistant referencing proprietary implementation guides, internal processes, and customized runbooks per customer. Each customer's documents must stay fully isolated from other tenants — no organization can gain visibility into another's IP. Legal also requires that no customer-provided documents are used to train or improve the underlying models, while the assistant still generates grounded responses.
options: A) Bedrock Knowledge Bases store/index each customer's docs in ISOLATED data stores, configure RESOURCE-BASED POLICIES so only that customer's assistant can retrieve embeddings/context; leverage Bedrock's native privacy guarantee (no training use), ground responses EXCLUSIVELY from the customer's isolated KB

B) Provide each customer's documents DIRECTLY to the model at RUNTIME, control exposure via customer-specific KMS key encryption; allow the FM to generate grounded answers reading UNPROCESSED documents, leverage output postprocessing to prevent leaks

C) Create a SEPARATE vector index per customer inside Bedrock Knowledge Bases but allow the backend to SHARE a common retrieval role that can access ALL indexes; depend on the APPLICATION LAYER to filter retrieved content by customer ID

D) Store customer documents in separate LOGICAL indexes inside Bedrock Knowledge Bases while allowing all indexes to SHARE a single underlying storage location and UNIFIED access policy for simplified management; depend on APPLICATION-SIDE ROUTING to direct queries to the correct customer context
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Third of four in this group — a THIRD access-control dimension alongside 077 (network path) and 078 (identity/authZ path): this one is DATA-LEVEL isolation between tenants inside Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The correct pattern is genuinely separate KBs (isolated data stores) with resource-based policies enforcing that each customer's assistant can only reach its own KB — isolation enforced at the RESOURCE/POLICY layer, not after the fact. Both traps (C and D) keep some surface-level separation (separate index, separate logical index) but undermine it with a SHARED retrieval role or SHARED underlying storage/policy, then try to patch the gap with application-layer filtering or routing — the same anti-pattern as trusting app code to enforce what the infrastructure layer should enforce, seen elsewhere in this exam (e.g., 049's rejected 'merge in application layer' retrieval design). Compare to 080, which governs data isolation for a SINGLE org's regulated fields rather than SaaS multi-tenancy.
explanation: Separate, isolated Bedrock Knowledge Bases per customer, combined with resource-based policies restricting retrieval to that customer's own assistant, enforce tenant isolation at the infrastructure/policy layer — no cross-tenant retrieval path exists to begin with. Bedrock's native guarantee that customer-provided data is never used to train or improve the underlying foundation models satisfies the legal requirement without any additional custom controls. B) sends raw, unprocessed documents directly to the model at runtime — encryption at rest doesn't prevent exposure once decrypted for inference, and output postprocessing can't guarantee no sensitive content ever surfaces. C) and D) both introduce a shared access path (a common retrieval role, or shared storage/unified policy) and then rely on the APPLICATION layer to filter or route correctly — but the retrieval call itself can already expose cross-tenant content before any filter runs, and a single misconfiguration collapses the isolation entirely.

question: Healthcare analytics group preps structured clinical data and semi-structured notes as a retrieval source for a Bedrock Knowledge Base. Regulatory officers require certain diagnosis codes and patient identifiers to be visible ONLY to a small compliance group, while de-identified aggregates can be used by the general data science team.
options: A) Lake Formation TABLE LEVEL permissions + Athena VIEWS to mask sensitive fields; grant BOTH compliance and data science teams access to the SAME tables, use SQL filters to remove restricted records during retrieval

B) Lake Formation table-level access grants + TWO Data Catalog entries separating sensitive/non-sensitive fields; compliance queries BOTH catalogs, data science sees only the non-sensitive catalog; Bedrock Knowledge Base 'automatically filters restricted cells' during retrieval

C) Store clinical datasets in S3 with DEFAULT bucket-level permissions, use IAM identity policies to restrict access to sensitive diagnosis codes; Bedrock Knowledge Base retrieves directly from S3, relying on IAM to enforce visibility at runtime

D) Lake Formation COLUMN level, ROW level, and CELL level permissions on the clinical datasets, fine-grained access granted ONLY to the compliance group for sensitive diagnosis codes/identifiers; data science team accesses de-identified columns and aggregated rows; Bedrock Knowledge Base queries only the permitted views
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Fourth of six in this group — pairs closely with 079, but the isolation boundary is different: 079 separates data between different CUSTOMERS (SaaS multi-tenancy) using separate Bedrock Knowledge Bases; this one separates data between different ROLES within a SINGLE organization (compliance vs. data science) at the FIELD level (specific columns/rows/cells within the same clinical dataset), using Lake Formation governance upstream of ingestion. Trap B is the sharp one: splitting into two Data Catalog entries LOOKS like fine-grained separation, but table-level grants on either catalog still expose whatever is in that table wholesale — true column/row/cell-level enforcement requires Lake Formation's actual fine-grained permission types, not catalog-level splitting. It also wrongly assumes Bedrock Knowledge Bases can 'automatically filter restricted cells' on Lake Formation's behalf — the KB isn't a substitute for the governance layer. 081 and 082 round out the group with two more angles: dedicated per-tenant vector collections at SaaS scale, and controlled cross-account retrieval without duplicating data.
explanation: Lake Formation's column-level, row-level, and cell-level permissions let you grant the compliance group exclusive access to sensitive diagnosis codes and patient identifiers, while the data science team only ever sees de-identified columns and aggregated rows — with the Bedrock Knowledge Base querying only the views each group is permitted to see. A) table-level permissions plus Athena view masking still leave the underlying tables accessible, and SQL-level masking isn't a substitute for real column/row/cell controls on regulated clinical data. B) splitting into two Data Catalog entries doesn't provide true fine-grained enforcement — without column/row/cell-level Lake Formation controls, table-level access still exposes full datasets, and Bedrock Knowledge Bases has no mechanism to filter restricted cells on Lake Formation's behalf. C) IAM identity policies and default S3 bucket permissions are too coarse to express column- or row-level restrictions required for regulated healthcare data.

question: A startup is building a multi-tenant SaaS knowledge assistant that uses retrieval augmented generation on Amazon Bedrock to provide customer-specific answers. Each customer uploads proprietary documents stored as embeddings inside a vector database for semantic search. The platform must scale to thousands of tenants while ensuring strict data isolation, encryption, secure cross-tenant access control, and predictable performance for each customer.
options: A) Export all tenant documents to S3, use a CENTRALIZED Bedrock Knowledge Base to generate embeddings for EVERY tenant in ONE unified vector store; apply METADATA-BASED FILTERING inside the Knowledge Base to ensure queries return only tenant-relevant results

B) Deploy a SEPARATE Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector for EACH tenant so embeddings remain fully isolated at the database level; integrate each cluster with a shared retrieval service that connects to the correct cluster based on the tenant identifier

C) Create DEDICATED vector collections or namespaces PER TENANT using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and enforce tenant isolation with resource policies, encryption by default, and fine-grained IAM controls; route all customer queries through a multi-tenant-aware retrieval layer that selects the correct collection based on the authenticated tenant identity

D) Store ALL tenants' embeddings in a SINGLE SHARED OpenSearch Serverless vector collection and tag each vector with a tenant ID for filtering; rely on CLIENT-SIDE application logic to filter out results that do not match the active tenant
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Fifth of six in this group — the OpenSearch-Serverless-flavored twin of 079: that question solves per-customer SaaS isolation using separate Bedrock Knowledge Bases with resource-based policies; this one solves the exact same problem using OpenSearch Serverless directly (dedicated collections/namespaces per tenant + resource policies + IAM), when the team owns its own vector store rather than delegating to Bedrock KB, and needs to scale cleanly to THOUSANDS of tenants. Trap D repeats 079's own rejected pattern almost verbatim: a shared collection tagged by tenant ID, with isolation enforced only by APPLICATION-LAYER filtering — the same 'trusting app code to do the infrastructure's job' anti-pattern flagged there. Trap B shows the opposite extreme: full per-tenant database isolation (a dedicated Aurora pgvector cluster each) is airtight but operationally unworkable at SaaS scale — useful to recognize when 'more isolation' stops being the right answer because it can't scale.
explanation: OpenSearch Serverless natively supports dedicated vector collections or namespaces per tenant, so each customer's data lives in a genuinely separate, access-controlled store; resource policies and default encryption prevent unauthorized access, fine-grained IAM enforces who can reach which collection, and a multi-tenant-aware retrieval layer uses the authenticated tenant's identity to route each query to the correct collection — real isolation enforced at the infrastructure layer, with predictable performance and clean scaling to thousands of tenants. A) centralizing everyone into one Bedrock KB and relying on metadata filters risks cross-tenant exposure the moment a filter is misconfigured, and prevents tuning performance per tenant. B) a dedicated Aurora pgvector cluster per tenant gives strong isolation but doesn't scale operationally to thousands of customers — provisioning, patching, and managing that many clusters contradicts the goal of centralizing infrastructure and controlling cost. D) a single shared collection tagged by tenant ID puts all isolation responsibility on application-layer filtering — a misapplied or bypassed filter leaks data across tenants, which is exactly the multi-tenant security anti-pattern this exam repeatedly flags.

question: A large enterprise has centralized all foundation model inference inside a dedicated AI platform account that runs Amazon Bedrock models behind a controlled access layer. Individual business units maintain their own OpenSearch Serverless vector collections and Aurora PostgreSQL clusters with pgvector in separate AWS accounts. A new initiative requires the Bedrock-based assistant in the AI platform account to retrieve context directly from these remote vector indexes without duplicating embeddings or moving the underlying data into the AI platform, while preserving strict cross-account security boundaries and minimizing operational overhead.
options: A) Expose the business unit vector indexes through CROSS-ACCOUNT IAM permissions supported by OpenSearch Serverless or Aurora pgvector and connect the AI platform account using AWS PRIVATELINK for secure, private retrieval; the Bedrock-based assistant issues vector similarity queries ON DEMAND while the data remains in the owner accounts

B) Export all embeddings and source metadata from each business unit into S3 in the AI platform account and REBUILD new OpenSearch Serverless vector collections centrally; schedule periodic Lambda sync jobs to refresh the centralized collections as new documents arrive

C) Ingest all business unit documents into a CONSOLIDATED Bedrock Knowledge Base inside the AI platform and let Bedrock generate NEW embeddings for all content; remove the need for cross-account connectivity entirely by relying only on the consolidated Knowledge Base for retrieval

D) Build a single Amazon API Gateway endpoint in the AI platform account that PROXIES requests to all business unit indexes across accounts; require each FM application to pass an index identifier so the gateway can forward the query to the correct backend
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Sixth and last in this group, and a subtle but important shift in GOAL from every other member: 077-081 are all about PREVENTING inappropriate access (locking down network paths, identities, tenants, fields). This question is about ENABLING appropriate access ACROSS an account boundary — a central AI platform account needs to query vector data that different business units deliberately keep in their OWN AWS accounts — while still avoiding data duplication and preserving each business unit's ownership and governance. The toolkit is genuinely the same (cross-account IAM, PrivateLink, resource-level policies on OpenSearch Serverless — the same service featured in 081) but the design goal flips: least-privilege ENABLEMENT rather than lockdown. Every wrong option solves the problem by DUPLICATING or CENTRALIZING data instead of querying it in place: B) exports and rebuilds collections centrally, C) reingests and fully re-embeds everything into one consolidated KB, and D) proxies through a single API Gateway that still requires cross-account data access to be resolved somewhere — none of them honor the 'without duplicating embeddings or moving data' requirement the way direct, in-place cross-account retrieval does.
explanation: Cross-account IAM permissions on OpenSearch Serverless (or Aurora pgvector) combined with AWS PrivateLink let the AI platform account issue vector similarity queries directly against each business unit's own index over a private, secure connection, on demand — the data never leaves its owning account, no embeddings are duplicated, and each business unit retains full control over its own vector store while still supporting efficient retrieval for the central Bedrock assistant. B) exporting and rebuilding centralized collections duplicates large datasets, adds storage/ingestion cost, and introduces synchronization lag between the source and the copy. C) reingesting everything into one consolidated Bedrock Knowledge Base forces a full re-embedding of content that already has embeddings elsewhere, strips business units of autonomy over their own data, and complicates governance across a large multi-account environment. D) a single central API Gateway proxy still has to resolve and route to the correct backend index per request, weakening fine-grained per-business-unit access control and creating a single point that breaks the account-level isolation the enterprise wants to preserve.

question: A cross-border law firm's e-discovery system runs ON-PREMISES because case evidence cannot leave the data center; the application is allowed to send SELECTED prompt excerpts to Bedrock in an approved Region for summarization. The data center already has private connectivity to a VPC there. Invoke models without routing API traffic over the public internet, minimizing custom networking components.
options: A) Advertise the connected VPC CIDR to the data center; forward on-prem DNS to Route 53 Resolver INBOUND endpoint IPs; IAM policies for Runtime actions; keep calling the REGIONAL RUNTIME HOSTNAME (no interface endpoint)
B) Deploy an HTTPS PROXY in the connected VPC; on-prem DNS resolves the runtime hostname to the proxy; proxy calls the regional runtime endpoint
C) Interface VPC endpoint for the Bedrock CONTROL service (wrong service — management APIs, not Runtime); private DNS; Resolver inbound; endpoint policy for Runtime actions
D) Interface VPC endpoint for the Bedrock RUNTIME service; enable private DNS; forward on-prem DNS to Route 53 Resolver INBOUND endpoint IPs; endpoint policy for required Runtime actions
group: Access Control, Identity & Data Isolation for Bedrock
comparison_note: Directly extends this group's existing PrivateLink member, adding two sharper failure modes: private VPC connectivity ALONE doesn't create a private path (trap A — AWS service hostnames don't automatically route via PrivateLink without the interface endpoint), and the CONTROL-plane endpoint (management APIs) is a different service from the RUNTIME endpoint that InvokeModel/Converse actually need (trap C). Trap B's proxy adds custom infrastructure the requirement explicitly wants minimized, and still needs the runtime interface endpoint underneath to actually be private.
explanation: An interface VPC endpoint for the Bedrock RUNTIME service (powered by PrivateLink) is what InvokeModel, Converse, and streaming operations actually use; enabling private DNS and forwarding on-premises DNS queries to the Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint IP addresses lets standard SDK calls from the data center resolve to private endpoint addresses with no custom proxy layer. A) private routing to the VPC alone doesn't make the regional service hostname resolve through PrivateLink without the runtime interface endpoint and private DNS in place. B) a proxy adds a custom networking component the requirement wants minimized, and its own outbound call still isn't private unless it ALSO uses the runtime interface endpoint. C) the Bedrock control-plane endpoint serves management operations, not runtime invocations like InvokeModel or Converse.

question: A water utility launches an internal assistant across several AWS accounts; engineers authenticate via an enterprise SAML IdP. Some users need Bedrock CONSOLE access to manage prompt resources; application workloads use SDK calls to invoke ONLY approved models. Prevent UNAPPROVED models from being used even at first invocation, and avoid unnecessary permissions for API-only workloads.
