C) Converse with an inline guardrail; publish SIMPLECOV files (wrong format — that's a code-coverage format, not test results) as prompt test results; load secrets from Secrets Manager; enable stage rollback
D) Converse + call ApplyGuardrail ONLY AFTER the response is returned (post-hoc, not enforced throughout); publish JUnit XML; trigger rollback of the SOURCE STAGE (not rollbackable) from EventBridge
group: Bedrock Prompt Management: Governance vs. Structured Engineering
comparison_note: A CI/CD-PIPELINE-mechanics companion to 107's testing-harness focus: same underlying goal (automated prompt/guardrail regression before release) but this question is about the release ENGINEERING details — CodeBuild report FORMAT, secrets handling, and rollback SCOPE. Three independent traps: env-var secrets (leak risk), the wrong report format (SimpleCov is coverage, not test results), and a source stage that simply cannot be rolled back.
explanation: Converse gives one common message interface across supported chat models with a guardrail attached to the inference request; CodeBuild report groups can publish JUnit XML as a supported test-report format; resolving secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store (rather than plaintext build variables) keeps credentials out of logs; and scoping rollback to the deployment stage restores only what failed. A) provider-specific InvokeModel bodies lose the common chat abstraction, environment-variable credentials risk exposure, and restarting the whole pipeline is unnecessarily disruptive. C) SimpleCov is a code-coverage report format, not the right format for prompt regression test results. D) checking the guardrail only AFTER the response is returned doesn't enforce it throughout the inference path, and a pipeline's source stage isn't a valid rollback target.

question: A museum team's exhibit-explanation prompts (variables for exhibit text, visitor age range, requested tone) show that changes improving one AUDIENCE sometimes DEGRADE another. They want an evaluation-based feedback LOOP that automatically REWRITES the prompt, grades outputs against representative samples, and compares the original and optimized prompts across THREE supported Bedrock models with minimal custom orchestration.
options: A) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging; analyze CloudWatch logs for prompt outcomes; MANUALLY revise the prompt template after each test run
B) Run an Amazon Bedrock ADVANCED PROMPT OPTIMIZATION job with JSONL prompt templates, evaluation samples, matching variables, an evaluator, and the three target models
C) Create prompt variants in Prompt Management; test each in the prompt builder; version the BEST-PERFORMING variant for reuse
D) Call the simple Bedrock OPTIMIZEPROMPT API separately for EACH target model; compare the returned optimized prompts using the same evaluation samples
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Bedrock Prompt Management: Governance vs. Structured Engineering
comparison_note: Introduces a distinct capability from this group's version/governance/regression-harness members: Advanced Prompt Optimization is a self-contained rewrite-grade-repeat LOOP across MULTIPLE models. Trap D is the sharpest — the SIMPLE OptimizePrompt API is a fast heuristic single-prompt, single-model rewrite with no evaluation data and no multi-model comparison, easily confused with the Advanced capability by name alone.
explanation: Advanced Prompt Optimization injects evaluation samples into prompt-template variables, sends them to the target model(s), grades outputs by the selected evaluation method, rewrites the prompt, and repeats — directly matching the requirement for an automated rewrite-and-grade loop compared across three models. A) invocation logging supports human analysis and monitoring but doesn't automatically rewrite or grade prompts. C) Prompt Management variants and console testing are interactive authoring tools, not an automated evaluation-data-driven optimization loop. D) simple prompt optimization is a fast heuristic rewrite for ONE short prompt and ONE model — it doesn't use evaluation data and doesn't optimize across multiple models.

question: Compliance team processes tens of thousands of PDF reports nightly, uploaded to S3 throughout the day, needing concise GenAI summaries ready by morning. Must avoid long synchronous API calls, handle failures for individual documents, and automatically retry only failed items without reprocessing the whole batch.
options: A) Nightly Step Functions EXPRESS workflow using a SINGLE Lambda task to scan S3 for all new PDFs, call Bedrock in large batches, write all summaries back to S3; a Retry policy on that Lambda task causes the ENTIRE batch job to rerun from the beginning on any error

B) Configure S3 to send document upload events to SQS; an EventBridge schedule starts a Step Functions STANDARD workflow that consumes the queue each night with a MAP STATE over document identifiers — each Map item invokes Lambda to fetch the PDF from S3, calls Bedrock for summarization, writes the summary back to S3, and applies PER-ITEM retry policies so only failed documents run again
C) S3 event notifications trigger a Lambda function for EVERY new PDF; the function calls Bedrock SYNCHRONOUSLY to generate a summary and store it in S3

D) AWS Glue job runs each night, crawls S3 for new PDFs, calls Bedrock from within a SINGLE Spark driver script that loops over all documents; the script writes summaries back to S3 and RERUNS THE ENTIRE Glue job if any error appears in the nightly logs
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Step Functions Batch, Pipeline Resilience & Human Review Orchestration
comparison_note: First of three in this new group. The defining requirement here is PER-ITEM retry at genuine scale (tens of thousands of independent documents) — a Step Functions Standard workflow's Map state fans out one branch per document, each with its own retry policy, so a handful of failures never force a reprocess of the whole night's batch. Every wrong option ties the whole job's fate to a SINGLE task or script: A) one Lambda scanning/batching everything with one retry policy, D) one Glue/Spark script looping over every document, C) no orchestration at all — thousands of independent per-upload Lambda invocations with no centralized retry or fan-out control. Compare to 111, which applies the complementary PER-STEP (not per-item) retry/catch pattern across a multi-stage pipeline, and 112, which adds a human-review stage into a similar Step Functions backbone.
explanation: S3 event notifications feeding SQS decouple ingestion from processing and smooth the day's upload spikes; an EventBridge-scheduled Step Functions Standard workflow then reads document identifiers and fans out via a Map state, one branch per document, each invoking Lambda to fetch the PDF, call Bedrock, and write the summary back to S3. Map state's item-level retry and error handling means only the documents that actually failed get reprocessed, with clear per-document status. A) an Express workflow with one Lambda task looping over the whole batch ties every document's fate to a single retry policy — one failure reruns everything. C) triggering Lambda synchronously per upload gives no centralized orchestration, poor observability across tens of thousands of invocations, and no clean way to retry only failed items for a scheduled nightly run. D) a single Glue/Spark script looping over every document means any exception fails the whole job, forcing a full rerun that reprocesses already-completed work.

question: Educational company's multi-step GenAI pipeline (generate quiz questions from course materials → validate → publish) sometimes fails from malformed source content, model timeouts, or quota issues. Need end-to-end visibility into where failures occur, automatic retries with backoff for transient errors, routing of permanently failed items to a dead-letter queue, and centralized logs/metrics for troubleshooting.
options: A) EventBridge triggers a series of INDEPENDENT Lambda functions chained by events; each Lambda writes status messages into an S3 bucket; leverage AD HOC log searches in CloudWatch Logs and MANUAL inspection of S3 status files to identify and retry failed items

B) A Step Functions STANDARD workflow wraps EACH GenAI step in states with RETRY for transient errors and CATCH that routes unrecoverable failures to an SQS dead-letter queue; enable CloudWatch Logs and Metrics for the state machine and integrate AWS X-Ray tracing on Lambda tasks and model calls for full visibility into latency and failure patterns
C) An SQS queue feeds a fleet of EC2 worker instances running a CUSTOM GenAI processing script; push application logs to CloudWatch Logs for troubleshooting

D) Place ALL GenAI logic into a SINGLE Lambda function that processes each item end to end; leverage Lambda's automatic retries and a dead-letter queue for failed invocations; configure basic CloudWatch alarms on function errors for monitoring
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Step Functions Batch, Pipeline Resilience & Human Review Orchestration
comparison_note: Second of three, and the complementary pattern to 110: that question fans out one Step Functions branch PER DOCUMENT (Map state) in a batch job. This question wraps EACH STAGE of a multi-step pipeline (generate → validate → publish) with its OWN Retry (for transient errors like timeouts/throttling) and Catch (routing permanent failures to an SQS DLQ), plus CloudWatch + X-Ray for step-by-step visibility into exactly where and why something failed. Trap D is the sharpest: it does have Lambda-level retries and a DLQ, but collapsing every stage into ONE function means you can never tell whether generation, validation, or publishing actually failed — retry/DLQ only operate at the whole-function level, not per logical step. A) and C) both push error handling and status-tracking into scattered, ad hoc, manually-inspected artifacts (S3 status files, plain CloudWatch logs) instead of a structured, queryable workflow.
explanation: A Step Functions Standard workflow lets each stage of the pipeline be its own state with a tailored Retry policy (exponential backoff on transient errors like model timeouts or throttling) and a Catch handler that routes unrecoverable failures — like malformed source content — to a dedicated SQS dead-letter queue with contextual metadata. CloudWatch Logs and Metrics on the state machine, plus X-Ray tracing across the Lambda tasks and model calls, give a clear, queryable, end-to-end view of exactly which stage failed and why. D) one monolithic Lambda hides all internal steps behind a single retry/DLQ boundary — there's no way to distinguish a generation failure from a validation failure. C) SQS+EC2 workers require building all retry, error-handling, and monitoring logic by hand, with no native per-stage visibility. A) chaining independent Lambdas via EventBridge with status written to S3 scatters state across files and logs, forcing manual investigation instead of centralized, structured error handling.

question: Legal consultancy's AI-driven clause drafting system must route every generated clause through mandatory human review. Attorneys evaluate each draft, provide structured feedback, and approve or request revisions. The firm also wants to capture feedback metadata to analyze revision categories, reviewer patterns, and long-term trends. The system must coordinate drafting, route human review tasks, trigger downstream processing, and store structured review data for long-term analysis.
options: A) Step Functions drafts clauses and IMMEDIATELY sends them to attorneys via an SNS topic WITHOUT involving Amazon Augmented AI (A2I); store lawyer feedback in a SINGLE S3 prefix and periodically run Athena queries to detect revision patterns

B) Step Functions orchestrates clause generation and routes cases to Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) for human review; configure A2I to send structured reviewer feedback to an Amazon EventBridge bus; write downstream consumers that store the feedback in DynamoDB with secondary indexes for long-term analysis; implement separate event patterns to handle approvals, rejections, and revision requests

C) Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) manages BOTH AI drafting AND human review, configured to store feedback ONLY in its managed output buckets; rely on manual exports from the A2I console to perform long-term trend analysis

D) Bedrock Agents manage the drafting and review process; configure Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) ONLY to notify attorneys by email when a clause is ready for review; store each reviewer comment as a separate S3 object for later analysis
group: Step Functions Batch, Pipeline Resilience & Human Review Orchestration
comparison_note: Third in this group, and a different SUB-PROBLEM than 110/111: those are about surviving failures (retrying documents, retrying pipeline steps). This one is about routing MANDATORY HUMAN REVIEW into the same Step Functions backbone using Amazon A2I (the purpose-built human-review-loop service), then treating each reviewer decision as a structured EVENT (via EventBridge) that fans out to multiple independent consumers — one of which persists to DynamoDB with secondary indexes for genuine analytical querying (revision categories, reviewer patterns, trends). Every wrong option breaks a different piece of that chain: A) skips A2I's structured review entirely (plain SNS + unstructured S3 + periodic manual Athena queries); C) lets A2I own drafting too (outside its purpose) and leaves feedback stuck in unindexed managed buckets needing manual export; D) demotes A2I to a mere email notifier and scatters feedback across individual S3 objects with no queryable structure.
explanation: Step Functions orchestrates the stateful drafting workflow while Amazon A2I — purpose-built for integrating human decisions into AI processes — manages the structured review step, ensuring consistent reviewer input; routing A2I's output through EventBridge creates an event-driven layer where separate event patterns can independently handle approvals, rejections, and revision requests; and storing the structured feedback in DynamoDB with secondary indexes gives the firm fast, flexible querying for trend reporting and reviewer-behavior insights. A) bypasses A2I's structured review entirely — SNS just notifies, it can't enforce structured feedback capture or guarantee review happens before approval, and S3-plus-periodic-Athena is high-overhead and not real-time. C) uses A2I for drafting too (not its purpose) and its managed output buckets aren't built for analytical querying — manual console exports don't scale for ongoing trend analysis. D) reduces A2I to an email notifier, losing its structured review capabilities, and storing each comment as a separate S3 object gives no attribute-level indexing for efficient trend analysis.

question: A university admissions team's interactive Bedrock assistant (behind API Gateway/Lambda) must collect missing applicant details before invoking the FM. Applicants often pause for SEVERAL HOURS between messages, and any STATELESS Lambda worker must be able to continue the conversation. An existing Comprehend custom classification endpoint maps utterances to intent classes synchronously. LEAST custom orchestration code.
options: A) Persist session context + CALLBACK TOKENS in DynamoDB; classify with Comprehend; coordinate clarification with STEP FUNCTIONS EXPRESS tasks before invoking Bedrock
B) Persist session context + pending prompts in DynamoDB; classify with Comprehend; coordinate clarification with Step Functions STANDARD Wait states + LAMBDA POLLING before invoking Bedrock
C) Persist session context + callback tokens in DynamoDB; classify with Comprehend; coordinate clarification with Step Functions STANDARD CALLBACK TASKS before invoking Bedrock
D) Persist session context in DynamoDB; INFER INTENT FROM BEDROCK PROMPTS (bypassing Comprehend); coordinate clarification with Lambda conditionals before invoking the Comprehend endpoint
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Step Functions Batch, Pipeline Resilience & Human Review Orchestration
comparison_note: A new sub-theme for this group alongside its existing A2I human-review member: the STEP FUNCTIONS CALLBACK (task-token) pattern for pauses that can last hours — pairs directly with 114's identical mechanism in a claims-review context. The recurring traps: EXPRESS workflows (trap A) don't fit multi-hour pauses at all, and Wait states + Lambda polling (trap B) adds exactly the custom orchestration code the callback task pattern is designed to avoid.
explanation: DynamoDB provides a durable session store any stateless Lambda invocation can read/update, including storing task tokens for pending clarification steps, while Step Functions STANDARD workflows support long-running orchestration with CALLBACK tasks — letting the next user message complete the waiting task directly via the stored token, with no polling loop. A) Express workflows are built for short-duration, high-volume runs and don't fit several-hour pauses. B) Standard workflows with Wait states can pause, but polling DynamoDB with Lambda adds custom logic the callback pattern avoids entirely. D) bypassing the existing Comprehend classifier and inferring intent from Bedrock prompts instead abandons a working pre-invocation classification step and moves logic into less predictable Lambda conditionals.

question: An insurance claims automation workflow drafts summaries/recommended actions with Bedrock, but HIGH-VALUE or LOW-CONFIDENCE cases need HUMAN ADJUSTER review before continuing — reviews can take SEVERAL DAYS. Collect the adjuster's decision/comments through an HTTPS endpoint WITHOUT keeping compute idle, with DURABLE and AUDITABLE orchestration. Pick two.
options: A) A STANDARD Step Functions workflow with a Lambda service integration using .waitForTaskToken, passing $$.Task.Token with the draft to the reviewer notification step
B) An API Gateway + Lambda callback endpoint that records the decision and calls SendTaskSuccess/SendTaskFailure with the task token FROM THE WORKFLOW ACCOUNT
C) An EXPRESS Step Functions workflow with a Lambda callback step, relying on the WORKFLOW TIMEOUT to cover multi-day reviews
D) A CROSS-ACCOUNT reviewer callback that calls SendTaskSuccess with the task token FROM THE REVIEWER TOOLING ACCOUNT
E) Store reviewer decisions in DynamoDB and use a SCHEDULED EventBridge rule to START A SEPARATE workflow that scans for approved claims
group: Step Functions Batch, Pipeline Resilience & Human Review Orchestration
comparison_note: The select-two API-level companion to 113's same pattern: pins down two mechanics not covered there — the TASK TOKEN must come from a principal in the SAME AWS ACCOUNT as the workflow (trap D fails this), and Express Workflows have a much shorter max execution duration, making trap C's 'rely on timeout' approach structurally wrong for multi-day reviews. Trap E swaps the direct callback resume for a polling reconciliation process — it avoids idle compute too, but adds latency and fragments the audit trail instead of resuming the original waiting execution.
explanation: A Standard Step Functions workflow using .waitForTaskToken pauses the state machine without keeping compute running, exposing the token via $$.Task.Token to the reviewer notification step; an API Gateway + Lambda callback endpoint then records the human decision and calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with that token — which must come from a principal in the SAME AWS account as the workflow. C) Express Workflows are built for short-running, high-volume work and don't support multi-day approval windows. D) Step Functions task tokens must be returned by same-account principals; a reviewer tooling system in a different account cannot use the token directly. E) scheduled polling avoids idle compute but replaces the direct callback resume with reconciliation logic, polling latency, and a fragmented audit trail instead of resuming the original waiting execution.

question: Customer support org receives thousands of unstructured issue descriptions daily, many containing sensitive personal details (phone numbers, addresses, account IDs). Need automated summarization that generates concise summaries WITHOUT exposing raw sensitive data to the FM. Sensitive elements must be identified/transformed/removed BEFORE summarization, and downstream teams must be able to audit how personal data was handled.
options: A) Amazon Comprehend PII detection tags detected entities; keep the ORIGINAL text intact so the FM can use full context during summarization; store redaction metadata separately, rely on DOWNSTREAM systems to mask sensitive fields AFTER the model completes its output

B) Data masking process using CloudWatch Logs Insights scans STORED support tickets and replaces sensitive values AFTER the content has already been processed by the model; forward model-generated summaries to downstream systems without additional filtering

C) Amazon Comprehend detects PII entities, sends BOTH the redacted AND original text to the FM so it can 'choose the best version' for summarization; store original content in a secondary location, rely on IAM policies to prevent unauthorized access

D) Amazon Comprehend PII detection as a PREPROCESSING step + a Lambda function AUTOMATICALLY redacts/replaces detected PII entities BEFORE passing sanitized text to the FM; only redacted versions are forwarded, detection metadata logged for compliance audits
see_also: Same detection tool (Amazon Comprehend PII) and redact-before-ingestion pattern as 029's RAG ingestion pipeline (PII redaction before chunking/embedding) — there the target was a vector index, here it's a summarization prompt, but the rule is identical: PII detection + Lambda redaction must happen BEFORE the FM (or the ingestion pipeline) ever sees the raw text, with detection metadata logged for audits. Contrast with 006, where the equivalent real-time protection is delivered natively through Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-information filters at invocation time, instead of a custom Comprehend+Lambda preprocessing step — use Guardrails when calling Bedrock directly and wanting built-in filtering; build a custom Comprehend+Lambda stage when PII must be scrubbed earlier in a pipeline (ingestion, preprocessing) before the FM is even invoked.
explanation: Running Comprehend PII detection as a preprocessing step, then using Lambda to automatically redact or replace every detected entity BEFORE the sanitized text reaches the foundation model, guarantees raw PII never enters the model — and logging detection metadata satisfies the compliance audit requirement. A) tags PII but leaves the ORIGINAL text intact for the model, only masking downstream after the fact — the model still sees raw PII, violating the core requirement. B) masks only after the model has already processed the content — the exposure already happened. C) sends both versions to the model 'so it can choose' — the original unmasked text still reaches the model, which is exactly what's prohibited.
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: First of three in this group — pairs with 116 (Macie discovery). This question redacts PII AT THE POINT OF USE: Comprehend detects entities in a stream of support tickets and a Lambda function scrubs them before a specific downstream pipeline (summarization) ever invokes the FM. 116 operates a level upstream and broader — discovering which of potentially hundreds of S3 locations even contain sensitive data in the first place, across an entire data estate, before any dataset is approved for GenAI use at all. 117 goes a level deeper still, into the specific ANONYMIZATION TECHNIQUES (tokenization, generalization, differential privacy) applied to structured research data.

question: Analytics organization has years of customer feedback across hundreds of S3 storage locations, with no inventory of which files contain sensitive details (personal identifiers, financial info, regulated content). The GenAI team wants to build fine-tuned models and retrieval pipelines from this data, but security requires automated visibility into sensitive-information presence before any dataset is used, plus a way to categorize, protect, and track risky files so only approved datasets flow into AI workflows.
options: A) Configure Bedrock Guardrails to block sensitive categories, rely on guardrail rules to detect/prevent PII from entering fine-tuning/retrieval datasets stored in S3; allow the RAG pipeline to ingest ALL S3 objects, depending on the guardrail filtering layer to ensure only compliant data is surfaced

B) Enable Amazon Macie across the relevant S3 buckets and configure automated sensitive data discovery jobs for FULL DISCOVERY to scan objects for PII and regulated patterns; use the classification findings to tag, quarantine, or restrict access to high-risk objects BEFORE allowing them into fine-tuning or RAG workflows

C) Enable Amazon Macie with DEFAULT monitoring; leverage automated OBJECT SAMPLING to identify sensitive files efficiently; use the PARTIAL findings to label only the detected objects and allow the REMAINING UNSCANNED data to flow into fine-tuning and retrieval pipelines

D) Use Amazon Athena to query SAMPLE objects from S3 and rely on pattern-matching queries to ESTIMATE which files might contain regulated fields; push all candidate datasets to a staging bucket and use IAM conditions to control downstream access during model training
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: Second of three in this group — pairs with 115. That question redacts PII AT THE POINT OF USE, per request, right before a specific pipeline (summarization) invokes the FM — a targeted, per-document sanitization step. This question is upstream and broader: DISCOVERING which of potentially hundreds of S3 locations even CONTAIN sensitive data in the first place, across an entire unstructured data estate with no existing inventory, before ANY dataset (fine-tuning or RAG) is approved for GenAI use. Trap C is the classic 'right tool, insufficient scope' pattern seen throughout this exam: it uses Macie, but DEFAULT monitoring only samples a subset of objects, and letting the unscanned remainder flow into training/retrieval pipelines defeats the entire governance purpose. Compare also to 080 (Lake Formation), which applies FIELD-LEVEL access control to already-cataloged STRUCTURED clinical data — a downstream access-control mechanism, not an upstream discovery/inventory mechanism for unstructured data of unknown content. 117 completes the group with the specific multi-technique anonymization pipeline (tokenization, generalization, differential privacy) that turns 'discovered/redacted' data into genuinely research-usable, privacy-preserving data.
explanation: Amazon Macie's automated sensitive data discovery, run as full discovery jobs across all relevant S3 buckets, uses managed detectors to build a complete, accurate inventory of PII and regulated content across a large, distributed, previously-uncatalogued data estate — the classification findings then drive tagging, quarantining, or access restriction on high-risk objects before they're ever allowed into fine-tuning or RAG workflows. A) Bedrock Guardrails operate at model invocation time (input/output filtering) and have no ability to scan or classify data at rest in S3 — they can't replace a data-at-rest discovery step, and letting the RAG pipeline ingest everything regardless still exposes sensitive content before any guardrail ever sees it. C) default monitoring with sampling only catches a subset of objects, and explicitly letting unscanned data flow into GenAI pipelines creates exactly the compliance gap the requirement was meant to close. D) Athena sampling queries can't reliably or continuously classify PII across an entire estate, and IAM conditions on a staging bucket don't identify sensitive content — they just gate access to whatever ends up there, scanned or not.

question: A healthcare research institute is building an internal analytics environment where data scientists ask natural language questions about long-term patient journeys, treatment paths, and outcomes. Strict privacy regulations prohibit sharing direct identifiers or easily linkable attributes with any external analytical system, including a new foundation model supporting exploration and early hypothesis generation. Pick two for a preprocessing pipeline that systematically masks and anonymizes data before it reaches the model, while still preserving enough utility for valid research.
options: A) Store only the fully transformed datasets in Amazon S3 and enforce that all model prompts and RAG workflows read from these anonymized S3 locations through tightly controlled IAM roles

B) Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block sensitive medical categories and set up guardrail rules to prevent identifiable patient details from reaching the foundation model during inference; allow the Lambda pipeline to pass RAW patient-level data to the model and leverage the guardrail layer to enforce privacy controls before the model processes the content

C) Build an AWS Lambda-based preprocessing pipeline that applies tokenization to direct identifiers, generalization to quasi-identifiers such as dates and locations, and differential privacy noise to aggregated metrics before invoking the foundation model

D) Build an AWS Lambda preprocessing workflow that tokenizes direct identifiers and applies light obfuscation to quasi-identifiers, then store BOTH the masked and partially masked datasets in S3 so the foundation model can choose the most suitable version during inference; allow downstream researchers to access both datasets through IAM roles while relying on CloudWatch logging to track how each dataset is used

E) Use AWS Lambda to copy all RAW patient records into a separate S3 bucket and enable server-side encryption and strict bucket policies, then allow the foundation model to read directly from this secured bucket for analysis; leverage encryption and access control to meet the requirement of preventing reidentification while preserving full data fidelity
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: Third in this group. 115 detects and redacts named PII entities (Comprehend + Lambda, tag-based) before a summarization prompt; 116 discovers/inventories WHERE sensitive data lives across an entire S3 estate (Macie, broad scan) before any dataset is approved for use. This question goes a level deeper into the ANONYMIZATION TECHNIQUE itself for structured/longitudinal research data: tokenizing direct identifiers, GENERALIZING quasi-identifiers (dates, locations — the auxiliary fields that enable reidentification even without a name), and adding calibrated DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY noise to aggregates, paired with an architectural rule that only the fully transformed data is ever reachable by the model (enforced via IAM, not just policy). Two traps share a subtle, recurring shape: B) reaches for Guardrails to 'enforce privacy controls' on RAW data passed to the model — Guardrails filters at inference time, it cannot anonymize or transform data beforehand, the same 'wrong layer' mistake as elsewhere in this exam. D) is the sharpest trap: it does real preprocessing but then keeps BOTH a masked AND a less-protected version reachable, letting the model or a researcher 'choose' — any path to the weaker version defeats the whole pipeline, echoing the strict single-tier access pattern in the access-control group's multi-tenant isolation lessons.
explanation: A Lambda pipeline applying tokenization to direct identifiers, generalization to quasi-identifiers like exact dates/ages/locations, and differential privacy noise to aggregated metrics gives layered, technique-appropriate protection — deterministic transformation of identifying fields plus a formal privacy guarantee on statistics — while storing only the resulting anonymized datasets in S3 and enforcing that every prompt and RAG workflow reads exclusively from those locations via constrained IAM roles creates a hard architectural boundary between raw and research-ready data. Together, these two options give both the RIGHT anonymization technique and the RIGHT access boundary. B) Bedrock Guardrails filters content at inference time — it cannot transform or anonymize the underlying data, so passing raw patient records to the model first and 'relying on Guardrails' still exposes identifiable data directly to the FM. D) preprocessing exists here, but keeping BOTH a masked and a partially masked (weaker) version reachable, with the model or researchers able to pick either, defeats the requirement that no identifiable or easily linkable data reach the model — the weaker copy is always one query away. E) encryption and bucket policies protect data at rest and in transit, but do nothing to prevent the model itself from receiving full-fidelity, directly identifiable patient records — encryption is not anonymization.

question: A wealth management firm's advisor-client chat summarizer must preserve financial issue, product names, and participant roles while MINIMIZING exposure of PII types and known ACCOUNT-NUMBER patterns to the FM and downstream users. Lambda processing is allowed; no custom ML model. Pick two.
options: A) Add PROMPT INSTRUCTIONS telling the FM to omit PII, with deterministic inference parameters
B) Configure a Bedrock guardrail with SENSITIVE-INFO FILTERS and CUSTOM REGEX PATTERNS, applied during model invocation
C) A Lambda preprocessing step calling Amazon Comprehend PII detection, replacing detected spans with STABLE PLACEHOLDERS before invoking Bedrock
D) Encrypt transcript objects with KMS; scope the invoking IAM role to decrypt only required S3 prefixes
E) Run Amazon Macie discovery on transcript buckets; send only objects WITHOUT sensitive-data findings to Bedrock
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: Reinforces the group's core two-layer pattern (pre-invocation Comprehend redaction PLUS Guardrails at invocation) with a select-two structure, echoed almost identically by 119's clinical-transcript version. Trap D repeats the recurring 'encryption is not anonymization' lesson — protecting data AT REST doesn't remove PII from what gets sent TO the model.
explanation: A Lambda preprocessing step using Comprehend PII detection to replace sensitive spans with stable placeholders (e.g., <CLIENT_NAME_1>) preserves useful context — participant roles, repeated references — without exposing original values, while a Bedrock guardrail with sensitive-info filters and custom regex (for organization-specific account-number formats) adds a managed policy layer at invocation. A) prompt instructions are not a reliable privacy boundary — the raw sensitive values are still in the prompt. D) KMS encryption and scoped IAM protect storage and access, but do nothing to remove PII from text sent to the FM. E) Macie's S3-level discovery isn't an inline per-request masking control, and filtering out every flagged object would reduce utility given how often these transcripts contain PII.

question: A university medical center's chatbot must reduce the chance PATIENT IDENTIFIERS or STUDY IDs reach the FM, enforce safety policy on BOTH prompts and generated responses, and allow REDACTION where possible rather than rejecting every request — minimizing custom model development and NOT relying on after-the-fact review as the primary control. Pick two.
options: A) A Lambda pre-processing step using Amazon Comprehend PII detection + pattern matching to redact patient identifiers/study IDs before invoking Bedrock
B) Enable CloudTrail logging for Bedrock activity and centralize events for compliance evidence and review
C) API Gateway request validator + a Lambda REGEX filter to enforce prompt schema and redact identifier-LIKE patterns
D) Attach a Bedrock guardrail to the model invocation with content filters, denied topics, sensitive-info handling, and response checks
E) Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3 protocol source buckets, tagging/quarantining objects BEFORE availability to the retrieval workflow
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: The clinical-domain twin of 118 — same correct pattern (Comprehend preprocessing + Guardrails at invocation), but with different distractors: CloudTrail (trap B) is auditability, not an inline content filter, and Macie (trap E) discovers sensitive data in stored S3 objects rather than filtering live prompts/responses in real time.
explanation: Comprehend-based Lambda preprocessing reduces PII exposure before the prompt reaches Bedrock, while a Bedrock guardrail applies safety policy to both input and output — together providing defense-in-depth without training a custom model, and allowing redaction/masking rather than blanket rejection. B) CloudTrail records API activity for audit purposes but performs no inline content filtering, so it cannot serve as the primary runtime safety layer. C) request validation and regex catch well-known formats but miss semantic PII (names, contextual identifiers) and provide no model-layer control. E) Macie discovers sensitive data already at rest in S3; it doesn't inspect live prompts or generated responses, and isn't a substitute for runtime redaction and guardrail enforcement.

question: A property insurance carrier's claims correspondence system must support quarterly SAFETY AUDITS. It must NOT retain RAW PII in logs/audit stores, must capture REDACTED prompt/response evidence, apply CENTRALLY MANAGED policy filters to BOTH input and output, and AUTOMATICALLY route suspected violations for COMPLIANCE REVIEW with minimal custom ML work.
options: A) Lambda pre/post processors that REDACT sensitive tokens; apply a Bedrock guardrail during invocation; write REDACTED records to CloudWatch Logs/S3; route violations via EventBridge to a Step Functions compliance workflow
B) Amazon Macie jobs classify the audit bucket (detection AFTER storage); apply a guardrail during invocation; write RAW interaction records; route Macie findings via EventBridge to Step Functions

C) API Gateway request validators reject malformed payloads (no content-safety check); tune Bedrock inference parameters (not policy enforcement); write FULL interaction records; route TIMEOUT events via EventBridge
D) Lambda pre/post processors HASH complete messages (destroys usable evidence); apply PROMPT INSTRUCTIONS (not centrally managed); write hashed records; route LOW-CONFIDENCE events via EventBridge
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: Extends the group's redaction pattern with an AUTOMATED COMPLIANCE-REVIEW-ROUTING layer (EventBridge → Step Functions), the same combination seen in 014 (this batch's insurance-claims Guardrails question in Group B). Every wrong option breaks exactly one half of the redact-then-enforce-then-route chain: raw storage before detection (B), no content filtering at all (C), or evidence-destroying hashing plus unmanaged prompt-only enforcement (D).
explanation: Lambda pre/post processors redact sensitive tokens before logging and after generation, a Bedrock guardrail provides managed input/output policy enforcement, redacted-only records satisfy audit needs without raw PII, and EventBridge routing violations to a Step Functions workflow decouples detection from human compliance review. B) stores RAW records before Macie detection runs — raw PII is already in the logs by the time anything is classified. C) has no content-safety filtering at all, only structural validation and inference tuning. D) hashing destroys the readable evidence reviewers need, and prompt instructions are not a centrally managed enforcement boundary comparable to Guardrails.

question: An online university's admissions app rewrites applicant messages containing PII. The team must ensure PII is NOT sent to FMs or captured in application-managed logs, enforce ZERO DURABLE RETENTION of FM request/response data by AWS or model providers, and PERMANENTLY DELETE all versions of audit objects in a VERSIONING-ENABLED S3 bucket after the retention period. Text responses only (no tool/function-call outputs).
options: A) Comprehend DetectPiiEntities per prompt; store returned OFFSETS WITH THE ORIGINAL TEXT (not redacted); Guardrails BLOCK; set provider_data_share retention; deny deletes via bucket policy before retention ends
B) Macie discovery jobs BEFORE batch processing; invoke Bedrock only for objects without findings; use DEFAULT Bedrock retention; S3 Lifecycle Expiration for CURRENT versions only

C) Comprehend DetectPiiEntities per request; REPLACE detected spans before logging/invoking Bedrock; set Bedrock data retention mode to NONE; apply Guardrails sensitive-info filters to responses; S3 Lifecycle expiring CURRENT and NONCURRENT versions

D) Guardrails sensitive-info filters with ANONYMIZE on prompts/responses; enable Bedrock invocation logging to S3 for RAW audit payloads; set store=false on Responses API calls; S3 Lifecycle expiring CURRENT versions only
group: Sensitive Data Discovery & Redaction for GenAI Pipelines
comparison_note: The capstone of this group — combines the Comprehend-redaction pattern (from 118/119) with two genuinely new, sophisticated mechanics: Bedrock's ZERO DATA RETENTION mode (retention='none', distinct from a generic 'don't store' setting or the fictional provider_data_share/store=false knobs in traps A/D), and S3 VERSIONING's NoncurrentVersionExpiration requirement — expiring only the CURRENT version (trap B/D) leaves old versions permanently recoverable in a versioning-enabled bucket.
explanation: DetectPiiEntities identifies PII locations so the application can REPLACE those spans before the content ever reaches Bedrock or application logs; setting Bedrock's data retention mode to none is the documented zero-retention control — request/response data isn't written to durable storage by AWS or shared with the model provider; Guardrails sensitive-info filters add defense-in-depth on text responses; and S3 Lifecycle rules must expire BOTH current and noncurrent object versions to permanently remove old data from a versioning-enabled bucket. A) storing offsets alongside the ORIGINAL (unredacted) text doesn't prevent exposure, and a bucket policy denying deletes is the wrong mechanism for lifecycle-based permanent deletion. B) Macie discovers sensitive data already at rest rather than filtering live prompts, default retention isn't zero-retention, and expiring only current versions leaves noncurrent versions recoverable. D) logging RAW payloads to S3 directly contradicts the goal, and store=false on a different API is not the same as Bedrock's documented zero-retention mode.

question: GenAI documentation assistant used by hundreds of internal teams shows wide variance in token usage across workloads. Finance needs accurate chargeback visibility across teams/projects/environments, and leadership wants strict token budgets for experimental workloads while still permitting higher limits for mission-critical applications.
options: A) Token metering layer logs input/output tokens for EVERY request through API Gateway, stores metrics in CloudWatch AND DynamoDB for per-tenant reporting; Lambda ENFORCES token budgets by evaluating usage BEFORE calling Bedrock, allows elevated limits for critical workloads through configurable policy rules

B) Aggregate cost data from AWS Billing and Cost Management console, rely on PERIODIC cost allocation tags to APPROXIMATE per-tenant token consumption; EventBridge rules notify teams when overall MONTHLY spending trends exceed thresholds

C) Build a centralized usage tracker recording token estimates in DynamoDB but allow teams to BYPASS budget checks by passing a PRIORITY FLAG in their API request; Lambda interceptor sends WARNINGS when teams exceed budgets INSTEAD OF enforcing hard limits

D) Token accounting layer records ESTIMATED token usage per request in DynamoDB, forwards PERIODIC summaries to CloudWatch Logs for reporting; Lambda SOFT enforces budgets by ALLOWING ALL requests to proceed while TAGGING overage attempts for later review
explanation: Logging input/output tokens at the API Gateway boundary for every request, storing metrics in both CloudWatch (dashboards/trends) and DynamoDB (granular per-tenant records), and having Lambda evaluate and enforce budgets BEFORE the Bedrock call actually happens — with configurable policy rules allowing pre-approved critical workloads to exceed standard limits — delivers both accurate chargeback visibility and real, proactive budget control. B) billing/cost-allocation tags only approximate spend at a coarse, periodic level — no token-level granularity and no real-time enforcement, so budgets can't actually be capped before overage happens. C) letting teams bypass enforcement with a self-asserted priority flag defeats governance entirely — warnings without hard limits provide no real control. D) 'soft enforcement' that lets every request proceed regardless and only tags overages after the fact never actually caps spending — it's observability, not budget enforcement.
group: Token & Cost Efficiency for GenAI Workloads
comparison_note: First in this small group — pairs with 123 (context-window optimization / prompt compression). This question is the GOVERNANCE side of token cost control: metering every request's token usage per tenant and enforcing hard budget limits before each Bedrock call, with configurable exceptions for critical workloads. 123 is the TECHNICAL EFFICIENCY side: actively shrinking how many tokens a RAG request needs in the first place, through smarter retrieval, compression, and pruning. Together they cover both halves of Domain 4's token-efficiency objective — track and cap spend, and reduce the spend that needs capping.

question: Research group's GenAI assistant answers questions over large technical reports that frequently exceed the FM's context limits. The current design forwards entire report sections into the prompt, driving up token usage, increasing latency, and often truncating important contextual clauses. Redesign context assembly and prompt construction to optimize context-window usage through pruning and compression while preserving the most relevant content.
options: A) Use Amazon Textract to extract all text from the documents and store complete sections in S3; feed these full sections into Bedrock by INCREASING the model's maximum token setting and rely on the model to handle truncation efficiently

B) Implement a retrieval pipeline that ranks passages using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, then apply PROMPT COMPRESSION techniques to summarize selected passages before injecting them into Bedrock for final inference; use DYNAMIC CONTEXT PRUNING so only the highest-relevance spans enter the final prompt

C) Adopt Amazon Comprehend to classify document sections and send ALL sections belonging to matching categories directly to Bedrock; avoid additional chunking logic because category-level grouping ensures the model receives broad thematic context

D) Implement a retrieval pipeline with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and forward ALL retrieved passages directly to Bedrock WITHOUT applying any summarization or compression; use a STATIC relevance threshold so all passages above the threshold are ALWAYS included for broader context coverage
domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Apps
group: Token & Cost Efficiency for GenAI Workloads
comparison_note: Second of three in this group — pairs with 122. That question TRACKS and BUDGETS token consumption per tenant after the fact (metering, chargeback, hard limits enforced before each Bedrock call). This question REDUCES token consumption per request in the first place, by combining retrieval ranking (only fetch the most relevant passages), prompt compression (summarize what's retrieved to shrink its token footprint), and dynamic pruning (adapt what actually enters the prompt to the query and current context load) — a technical efficiency strategy rather than a governance/budgeting one. Trap D is the sharpest: it uses the right retrieval service (OpenSearch Serverless) but skips compression entirely and uses a STATIC threshold that can't adapt to query length or content density — recall without cost control. Trap A doesn't use retrieval-based context selection at all, just brute-forces a bigger token limit and hopes truncation handles the rest. 124 adds a third token-management lever entirely: right-sizing the max_tokens RESERVATION itself to maximize throughput under Bedrock's quota burndown mechanics, rather than reducing what's sent to the model or tracking what's spent.
explanation: Ranking passages with OpenSearch Serverless narrows the field to the most relevant spans, applying prompt compression to summarize those selected passages shrinks their token footprint before they ever reach Bedrock, and dynamic context pruning adapts in real time to query and content load so only the highest-relevance spans make it into the final prompt — together minimizing tokens, latency, and the risk of truncating important clauses, without sacrificing semantic fidelity. A) feeding full extracted sections and simply raising the max token setting doesn't reduce token usage at all, and relying on the model to 'handle truncation efficiently' risks losing exactly the important contextual clauses the requirement wants preserved. C) category-level document classification with no chunking still forwards large blocks of text — it doesn't solve the context-limit problem, just re-buckets it. D) retrieval without any compression, plus a static relevance threshold that can't adapt to varying query/content patterns, still lets token usage grow unchecked and risks the same truncation problem.

question: A regional airline's customer operations team runs an interactive disruption-management assistant on Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API. During weather events, many requests are throttled by token quota even though the median generated answer is brief. The application currently sets a very large output-token limit on every request to avoid truncating rare long answers. The team must improve effective throughput without changing the API contract, moving to asynchronous processing, or buying dedicated capacity.
options: A) Route synchronous model calls through cross-Region inference profiles and keep the current output-token limit
B) Set request output-token limits from observed answer lengths and route rare long answers to a separate interaction path
C) Increase client-side concurrency and add exponential backoff for throttled requests from the runtime endpoint
D) Enable prompt caching for shared instructions and keep the current output-token limit for all user turns
domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Apps
group: Token & Cost Efficiency for GenAI Workloads
comparison_note: Third in this group, and a distinct token-management LEVER from both siblings: 122 tracks and budgets token SPEND per tenant after usage (governance/chargeback); 123 reduces how many tokens a RAG request actually needs by improving what gets retrieved and how it's compressed (context-window efficiency). This question is about neither spend-tracking nor context reduction — it's about the fact that Bedrock reserves quota using INPUT TOKENS PLUS THE CONFIGURED MAX_TOKENS at the START of every request, before generation even happens, so an oversized 'just in case' output-token limit silently reserves — and wastes — throughput capacity on every single call, even when the actual answer is short. Right-sizing max_tokens from observed answer lengths, with a separate path for the rare long response, directly attacks that upfront reservation. Every wrong option leaves the oversized reservation untouched: cross-Region inference profiles route bursts elsewhere but each request still reserves the same inflated quota; more client concurrency just exhausts the same quota pool faster; and prompt caching speeds up a shared prefix without touching the output-token side of the reservation at all.
explanation: Amazon Bedrock deducts total input tokens plus the configured max_tokens from quota at the start of a runtime request, replenishing unused quota only after processing completes — so setting max_tokens close to realistic, observed answer lengths (instead of a defensively large ceiling) directly reduces the quota each request reserves, freeing up effective throughput for more concurrent requests; routing the rare long-answer case to a separate interaction path preserves correct handling for those exceptions without inflating the reservation for the common case. Cross-Region inference profiles can help route around regional capacity constraints, but each request still carries the same oversized reservation regardless of which Region serves it. Increasing client concurrency doesn't add token budget — it just means the same fixed quota gets exhausted faster, worsening throttling rather than fixing it. Prompt caching reduces cost and latency for a repeated, stable input prefix, but it has no effect on the max_tokens portion of the quota reservation, which is exactly what's causing the bottleneck here.

question: A government agency needs a Policy Drafting Assistant that can synthesize complex legal materials (statutes, regulations, internal policy memos) into grounded draft proposals. The system must run entirely inside AWS GovCloud for data sovereignty, support asynchronous/batch-style workloads so analysts can request long-form policy drafts without waiting interactively, provide full traceability and grounded reasoning so reviewers can verify each generated insight, and minimize operational overhead due to limited infrastructure budgets. Pick two.
options: A) Deploy an ECS cluster running custom containers with open-source LLMs, mount encrypted EFS volumes containing legal materials; an internal API Gateway endpoint submits batch requests and streams outputs back through a CUSTOM response handler
B) Use Titan Text models available in AWS GovCloud together with Amazon Bedrock ASYNCHRONOUS model invocation to run long-form batch generation jobs

C) Host a large FINE-TUNED LLM on Amazon SageMaker GPU instances in GovCloud, process batch jobs using SageMaker Processing; CUSTOM LOGIC inside the inference container performs grounding by searching static documents in S3 and embedding them into prompts

D) Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a multi-step workflow that performs MANUAL retrieval from S3, constructs prompts inside Lambda functions, then calls the Bedrock InvokeModel API; split long-running workloads into multiple Step Functions states to generate drafts in segments
E) Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to ground outputs in statutes and internal memoranda, ensuring traceability and contextual relevance
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Data Sovereignty & Hybrid/Regional Deployment
comparison_note: First of two in this new group — pairs with 126. This question satisfies sovereignty by staying inside a SINGLE alternate AWS partition (GovCloud) built specifically for regulated US federal workloads, then layers Bedrock's managed asynchronous invocation on top for long-form batch drafting (no interactive latency budget to protect) plus Knowledge Bases for managed, traceable grounding. Traps C and D repeat two of this exam's most persistent lessons in a new setting: C reaches for SageMaker GPU hosting with hand-built retrieval/grounding logic — heavy ops, manual and error-prone grounding, exactly what 'minimize operational overhead' rules out; D reaches for Step Functions to manually assemble prompts and segment a long generation across states — Step Functions orchestrates steps well but was never built to carry large-context, long-form generation itself. 126 tackles a HARDER sovereignty case: not one federal jurisdiction inside a single AWS partition, but SEVERAL COUNTRIES simultaneously, each demanding data never leave its borders — a genuinely different architecture (Outposts, not a GovCloud-style partition).
explanation: Titan Text models running inside AWS GovCloud keep every stage of inference physically within the GovCloud boundary, satisfying data sovereignty; Bedrock's asynchronous model invocation is purpose-built for exactly this kind of long-form, non-interactive generation, freeing analysts from waiting on a live response; and Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingest the statutes, regulations, and internal memos so every generated insight can be traced back to an authoritative source — all as managed services with minimal operational burden. A) ECS with custom open-source LLM containers, EFS volumes, and a hand-built streaming response handler is exactly the heavy infrastructure footprint the agency wants to avoid. C) fine-tuning and hosting a large LLM on SageMaker GPU instances means owning GPU infrastructure, autoscaling, and inference logic, and rolling your own grounding by manually embedding S3 search results into prompts is error-prone compared to managed Knowledge Bases retrieval. D) Step Functions can chain steps, but manually assembling prompts in Lambda and splitting a long generation across state boundaries duplicates retrieval/grounding logic and isn't a natural fit for large-context model invocations.

question: A financial institution operates in several countries that require local processing of sensitive customer data, while central analytics and shared services run in an AWS Region. The GenAI platform team wants to deploy foundation model inference close to on-premises data for compliance, reduce latency for users in major metropolitan areas, and connect on-premises, edge, and regional environments using a unified routing and security design that respects strict data residency rules.
options: A) Use Local Zones in ALL countries for FM inference, connect on-premises systems to the Region through site-to-site VPN tunnels; add AWS Global Accelerator for traffic distribution and rely on routing policies to enforce data residency requirements

B) Deploy AWS Snowball Edge devices in each country to run inference workloads and periodically sync output to the central Region; use internet-based VPN connections to link metropolitan users with the nearest Snowball Edge location

C) Deploy AWS Outposts racks in each country to run foundation model inference locally and use AWS Direct Connect with Transit Gateway to integrate on-premises networks with the central Region; configure Local Zones in metro areas that require low latency and enforce residency controls using region-specific routing domains

D) Place all foundation model inference workloads in a single central Region and use AWS Wavelength Zones to serve metropolitan users with lower latency; backhaul all on-premises data to the Region through Direct Connect gateways for centralized processing and storage
group: Data Sovereignty & Hybrid/Regional Deployment
comparison_note: Second of three in this group — pairs with 125. That question satisfies sovereignty by running everything inside ONE dedicated AWS partition (GovCloud), a clean fit for a single federal jurisdiction with a batch/async workload. This question is the harder, MULTI-COUNTRY case: several countries simultaneously require inference to happen ON their own soil, plus real-time low-latency service for major metro users, plus secure hybrid connectivity back to a shared central Region — no single alternate partition solves that. AWS Outposts (physical AWS infrastructure racks placed inside each country) is the tool that actually keeps compute local per-jurisdiction, with Direct Connect + Transit Gateway providing the controlled, high-bandwidth hybrid network fabric, and Local Zones layered in only where metro latency additionally matters. Every wrong option reaches for a tool that sounds infrastructure-adjacent but doesn't actually guarantee residency: Local Zones (A) and Wavelength Zones (D) are both latency/edge tools with no data-sovereignty guarantee, and Snowball Edge (B) is built for temporary/disconnected/migration use cases, not continuous production inference. 127 closes the group with the lightest-weight approach of the three: Bedrock's own Cross-Region Inference GEOGRAPHIC profile, a managed, API-level mechanism for staying within a geographic compliance boundary while gaining burst resilience — no physical infrastructure or dedicated partition required.
explanation: AWS Outposts racks deployed inside each country let foundation model inference run physically within that country's borders — the only way to guarantee sensitive data and its processing never cross a jurisdiction's boundary — while Direct Connect paired with Transit Gateway builds a controlled, high-bandwidth hybrid network integrating each country's on-premises environment with the central Region, and Local Zones add low-latency presence in metro areas that need it, with region-specific routing domains enforcing which traffic stays where. A) Local Zones don't provide data residency guarantees at all — they're a latency tool, not a compliance boundary — and Global Accelerator/routing policies can't enforce jurisdiction-specific restrictions on their own. B) Snowball Edge devices are designed for temporary, disconnected, or migration workloads, not persistent, continuously available enterprise inference, and internet-based VPN to reach them adds latency and reliability risk that a regulated GenAI workload can't tolerate. D) Wavelength Zones optimize for mobile edge computing, not data sovereignty, and centralizing all inference in one Region while merely backhauling on-premises data violates the country-level residency requirement outright.

question: An online education platform's assessment integrity team uses Amazon Bedrock to generate incident summaries for schools in the European Union. The selected foundation model is directly invoked from one approved EU Region and supports an EU Geographic Cross-Region inference profile. Exam week traffic creates unplanned bursts that sometimes cause service disruption. Legal requirements state that model processing must remain within the EU geography, and the organization uses AWS Organizations SCPs to restrict access to unapproved Regions. The team wants to improve continuity with minimal application changes and without purchasing committed model capacity.
options: A) Use a GLOBAL Cross-Region system-defined inference profile, or create an application inference profile from it, invoke the profile as the model identifier, and allow aws:RequestedRegion UNSPECIFIED through SCPs

B) Use the supported EU GEOGRAPHIC Cross-Region system-defined inference profile, or create an application inference profile from it, invoke the profile as the model identifier, and allow ALL DESTINATION REGIONS in the profile through SCPs
C) Configure custom application routing to invoke the same model directly in multiple supported EU Regions, update the signing and endpoint logic, and allow those EU Regions through SCPs
D) Invoke the model directly in the current EU Region, add Step Functions retry handling, and return a queued status when regional invocation continues to fail
domain: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management and Compliance
group: Data Sovereignty & Hybrid/Regional Deployment
comparison_note: Third in this group, and by far the LIGHTEST-weight approach of the three: 125 (GovCloud) uses a dedicated AWS partition, and 126 (Outposts) deploys physical AWS infrastructure inside each country — both genuinely heavy infrastructure commitments. This question solves geographic compliance with a single Bedrock-native mechanism: a Cross-Region Inference GEOGRAPHIC profile (here, EU-bounded), invoked simply by specifying the inference profile as the model identifier — no new infrastructure, no custom routing code, just an API parameter and the matching SCP configuration. The trap between options A and B is exact and easy to miss: a GLOBAL profile can route to supported commercial Regions WORLDWIDE (wrong for an EU-only legal requirement, and its SCP pattern uses aws:RequestedRegion unspecified), while a GEOGRAPHIC profile stays bounded to a defined geography like the EU (right fit, and its SCP pattern instead requires allowing ALL destination Regions listed IN that specific profile) — same underlying Cross-Region Inference feature, two different profile types, two different SCP configurations, and only one of them actually enforces the residency boundary.
explanation: A Geographic Cross-Region Inference profile scoped to the EU routes burst traffic across multiple Regions within that defined geography without ever leaving it, satisfying the legal requirement to keep model processing inside the EU; the application invokes it exactly like any other model by specifying the inference profile as the model identifier, requiring minimal application change, and SCPs must be configured to allow all destination Regions listed in that specific profile. The Global profile option uses the wrong scope entirely — it can route to supported commercial Regions worldwide, which violates the EU-only legal requirement, and its distinct SCP pattern (allowing aws:RequestedRegion unspecified) is documented for global profiles, not geographic ones, so applying it here would be doubly incorrect. Custom multi-Region application routing could technically keep traffic within the EU, but it requires the application to own signing, endpoint selection, and retry logic across Regions — exactly the extra application complexity Bedrock's managed Cross-Region Inference profile is meant to eliminate. Retrying in place with Step Functions and returning a queued status may improve graceful degradation for transient failures, but it never actually adds access to compute capacity in another Region, so it doesn't solve the underlying burst-continuity problem.

Exam-week bursts cause unplanned service disruption. Legal requires processing to STAY WITHIN the EU; SCPs restrict access to unapproved Regions. B) The EU GEOGRAPHIC Cross-Region system-defined inference profile (or an application profile from it); invoke as modelId; allow ALL DESTINATION REGIONS in the profile through SCPs
